# PickIreland — full content

> Every buying guide on pickireland.best, in plain text: product specs, running costs at Irish electricity rates, pros, cons, verdicts and FAQs. This file is the complete corpus; llms.txt is the index.

Author: André Pires (Founder & Editor).

## Methodology
Products are compared on manufacturer specifications, verified owner feedback and Amazon.ie ratings, running costs calculated at Irish electricity rates, and suitability for Irish conditions and law. We do not physically test products; guides are research- and specification-based, and say so. Rankings are never influenced by affiliate commission.

## Key Ireland-specific figures used across these guides
- Domestic electricity day rate: ~€0.38/kWh (July 2026). Source: SEAI energy statistics (seai.ie/data-and-insights/seai-statistics/prices) and published supplier standard rates.
- Typical smart-meter night rate: ~€0.18/kWh, which roughly halves the running cost of anything scheduled overnight.
- E-scooter law (S.I. 199 of 2024): max 400W continuous output, max 20km/h design speed, max 25kg, wheels >=200mm. Source: irishstatutebook.ie.
- Cycle to Work scheme ceiling for e-bikes: €1,500 (2026).
- Mould needs sustained relative humidity above ~60%; target 50-55% indoors.

## How running cost is calculated
Cost per hour = rated watts ÷ 1,000 × €0.38 per kWh. It is a CEILING, not a measurement: thermostats and humidistats cycle the element or compressor off, so most appliances do not draw rated power continuously. Products whose manufacturer does not publish a rated wattage carry no running-cost figure — we do not estimate one. Running cost is only shown for mains appliances that run for sustained periods; it is omitted for battery products (e-bikes, e-scooters, robot vacuums, robot mowers) where cost per hour would be meaningless.

## How cost per charge is calculated
Cost of one full charge = battery capacity in Wh ÷ 1,000 × €0.38 per kWh, at the Irish domestic day rate. Unlike running cost this is a FLOOR, not a ceiling: it is the energy the battery stores, and the wall socket delivers a few percent more because charger losses are heat rather than capacity. Capacity is taken from the manufacturer spec, either as a published Wh figure or as nominal volts × amp-hours. Products whose battery capacity is not published carry no figure — we do not estimate one. Shown for e-bikes and e-scooters; robot vacuums and robot mowers publish no capacity, so they carry no figure.

# CATEGORY: Air Fryers
URL: https://pickireland.best/air-fryers/
5 guides, 36 product entries
==============================================================================

The air fryer conquered the Irish kitchen for one simple reason: with electricity prices among Europe's highest, heating a whole oven to cook for two people stopped making sense. A typical air fryer uses 50–70% less energy than a conventional oven for everyday meals — and does chips better. We compare every size and budget, from compact singles to dual-drawer family machines.

## Size by household
1–2 people: 3.5–5L. Families of 3–4: 6–8L or dual-zone. Batch cookers and big families: 9L+. Under-buying is the #1 regret in reviews — a too-small basket means cooking in frustrating rounds.

## Dual-zone or single?
Two drawers let you cook mains and sides simultaneously at different temperatures — the feature families keep once they've had it. Singles are cheaper, smaller on the counter, and fine for one or two people.

## Energy savings are real
An air fryer at ~1,500 W cooking for 20 minutes uses roughly 0.5 kWh (~18 cents). A fan oven preheated and run for 45 minutes uses 1.3–1.8 kWh (~45–65 cents). Cook five times a week and the machine pays for itself within a year or two.

## What actually matters
Skip the 12-preset marketing. What separates good from bad: drawer build quality, even cooking without shaking religiously, dishwasher-safe parts, and a max temp of 200°C+. Ninja dominates because it nails these four.

Full running-cost table for every air fryer we track: https://pickireland.best/air-fryers/air-fryer-running-costs-ireland.html

#### What actually makes an air fryer's air circulation work?
A real air fryer mounts a fan above a perforated basket, forcing hot air down and around the food rather than just heating a sealed drawer like a mini oven. Cheaper models fuse the element and fan into a single housing over a shallow basket, which browns the top layer well but leaves anything underneath steaming in its own moisture. Every countertop box now calls itself an air fryer, so the giveaway is basket depth relative to width: a wide, shallow basket spreads a single layer of chips or nuggets properly, while a deep, narrow one forces stacking, and stacking is what makes shaking halfway through non-negotiable rather than optional. Manufacturer figures rarely mention shake frequency, so check the basket photos before the spec sheet — a tall, letterbox-shaped drawer usually means interrupting the cook twice, not once.

#### Why doesn't the litre rating match what actually fits in the basket?
The litre figure on the box measures the basket's total volume, not the usable cooking space once you allow for airflow clearance around the food. A drawer rated at 4.2 litres realistically holds two adult portions of chips plus a protein item spread in a loose single layer, not stacked. For the typical Irish household, that means a couple is comfortable at 2-3.5 litres, a family of four wants 5.5-7.6 litres or a dual-zone split, and anyone regularly feeding five or more should look at 8 litres and up or accept cooking in two rounds. The honest test before buying is picturing a full tray of frozen chips, not a handful, sitting in a single layer inside that basket. If the listing photos only ever show the basket half full, that's usually because a genuinely full load doesn't circulate properly.

#### The real energy sum: air fryer versus oven
Run the numbers instead of trusting a marketing claim of 'up to 70% less energy.' An electric oven drawing roughly 2.5kW needs about 10 minutes to preheat plus a further 40 minutes cooking a typical tray bake — 50 minutes total, or 0.83 hours. At 2.5kW that's 2.08 kWh, and at the current average Irish unit rate of around 38 cent per kWh, that single meal costs roughly 79 cent in electricity alone. An air fryer at 1.6kW needs no preheat and typically finishes the same food in 20-25 minutes — call it 22.5 minutes, or 0.375 hours — for 0.6 kWh and about 23 cent. That's a saving near 56 cent every time you cook. Do that for five evening meals a week and the air fryer saves about €2.80 a week — roughly €12 a month, or €145 across a full year. Evening cooking sits inside peak hours on every tariff, so a smart meter's cheaper night rate doesn't change this particular comparison.

#### What breaks first on an air fryer?
Failure points on most machines cluster in three places: the non-stick coating on the basket, the drawer's slide mechanism, and the digital display. Coating wear shows up first on baskets used daily without a silicone liner or light oil spray, typically within 12-18 months of heavy use, and owner reports consistently mention recoating or replacing the basket as the reason a working machine eventually gets binned. The slide mechanism — plastic rails letting the drawer click in and lock — takes the most physical abuse from daily use and is the part most likely to loosen on budget models first. Under Irish and EU consumer law, appliances carry a minimum two-year manufacturer guarantee, and it's worth confirming the seller is EU-based before buying, since claims against UK-only retailers post-Brexit now involve customs friction that erodes any saving. A basket explicitly marked dishwasher-safe, rather than merely wipeable, is worth prioritising over almost any other spec.

#### Where the extra money actually buys something
Spend under €50 and you're generally buying a single-speed, dial-controlled basket with no shake reminder and a coating unlikely to survive two years of regular dishwasher cycles — fine for occasional use, frustrating for daily cooking. Between €60 and €110 is where digital controls, presets and a shake reminder become standard, and where build quality first turns genuinely reliable rather than a lucky draw. Above €110, the money increasingly buys dual-zone functionality, larger capacity or app connectivity rather than better core cooking, since crisping performance itself plateaus once the fan and basket geometry are competent. The exception is genuinely large households, where the jump to 8+ litres or a split basket solves a real batch-cooking problem rather than adding a feature nobody touches. Match the spend to the actual gap in your kitchen — capacity for families, reliability and simplicity for everyone else.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: How much does an air fryer actually cost to run per month in Ireland?
A: It depends on frequency, but a realistic middle case is five evening meals a week at roughly 0.6 kWh per cook and 38 cent per unit, working out to about 23 cent per meal, or €5-6 a month for a household cooking dinner this way five nights out of seven. Heavier use — daily cooking plus reheats and snacks — pushes that closer to €10-15 a month. Either figure sits well below running an oven for the same meals, where preheating alone typically adds 15-20 cent to every single use. The bigger monthly saving usually isn't the electricity itself, it's the meals that would otherwise have become a takeaway because the oven felt like too much effort for one portion.

Q: Is a more expensive air fryer actually better, or just bigger?
A: Past roughly €110, extra spend mostly buys capacity, a second independent zone, or connected features, not meaningfully better crisping. Forced-air cooking plateaus once a machine has a competent fan and a properly shaped basket, and both arrive well before the top of the price range. Higher prices are genuinely justified for households that need the extra litres or two simultaneous zones for real batch cooking; paying for capacity you'll use every week is different from paying for a badge on the front. Check basket dimensions and stated wattage before the price tag — two machines at €70 and €180 can heat almost identically and differ mainly in how much food they hold.

Q: Do I need a dual-zone air fryer, or is a single basket enough?
A: For one or two people, a single basket almost always covers it. Dual-zone earns its keep once you're regularly cooking a main and a side that finish at different times, which is mostly a three-plus person household problem. A single basket around 4.5-5.5 litres handles sequential cooking fine for smaller households — the second item goes in while the first rests, costing a few minutes rather than much at all. Buy dual-zone for the synchronised finish, not the extra capacity alone, since one large basket often holds close to as much food as two small zones combined once you account for the divider between them.

Q: Can an air fryer fully replace my oven?
A: For most weeknight cooking, yes — chips, nuggets, chicken pieces, roasted vegetables, reheating, even a fair amount of baking in the larger multi-cooker style units. Where it can't compete is anything needing real volume or specific oven geometry: a full roasting tray for six, a large cake tin, or dishes that need steady ambient heat around the food rather than direct airflow, like a big lasagne. Most Irish households that make the switch end up keeping the oven for Sunday roasts and big-batch cooking, and leaning on the air fryer for the other six days of the week. It replaces daily use convincingly; it doesn't replace the appliance itself for every job.

Q: How long do air fryers actually last before something goes wrong?
A: Two to four years of near-daily use is a realistic expectation before the basket coating degrades enough to need replacing or the unit itself develops a fault, based on the pattern across owner reviews at every price point. Machines under €50 tend to cluster at the low end of that range; models with metal internal components and a stated two-year warranty skew longer. The single biggest lifespan factor within your control is the basket coating — hand-washing with a soft sponge instead of abrasive pads or a harsh dishwasher cycle roughly doubles how long it stays properly non-stick before food starts catching on it.

Q: What's the single feature most worth paying extra for?
A: A shake reminder paired with an accurately proportioned basket, not a screen or app control. Uneven cooking is the most common complaint in Irish reviews, and it's almost always a shaking problem rather than a fundamental fault — either the owner forgot, or the basket's proportions made a proper shake impossible without half the contents landing on the counter. A timer that pauses and prompts partway through the cook solves this directly, and it's available on machines well under €100. Everything layered on top of that price point is convenience rather than an improvement in how the food actually turns out.

#### What do you actually lose buying an air fryer under €100?
Under €100, wattage typically drops from the 1700–1800W common on mid-range machines to 1000–1400W, which stretches cook times by roughly a third rather than ruining results, and controls move from a digital touchscreen with presets to a mechanical dial with no shake reminder. The non-stick coating is rarely cut, since decent coating is the cheapest component and common even at €30. Manufacturers hit a sub-€100 price by trimming specific things, not everything at once. Baskets shrink in depth before they shrink in width, since a shallow basket is cheaper to manufacture and still photographs well. What genuinely separates a good sub-€100 machine from a bad one is fan placement and basket shape, not the number printed on the box.

#### How can you tell a good cheap air fryer from a disposable one?
The split isn't really about price within this bracket, it's about three checks that take thirty seconds each. First, is the wattage a fixed number or a vague 'up to' figure — the latter usually means the stated wattage is a brief peak, not what the element actually draws while cooking. Second, does the listing explicitly say dishwasher-safe, or does it hedge with 'easy to clean,' which usually means hand-wash only and a coating that won't take repeated hot cycles. Third, is the basket sold as a spare part anywhere, which tells you whether the manufacturer expects the machine to still be running in two years. A €35 machine that passes all three checks will usually outlast a €70 machine that fails them, because price under €100 correlates weakly with durability and strongly with brand marketing spend.

#### Does a budget air fryer still beat the oven on cost?
Yes, and the gap barely narrows. A budget unit at 1.2kW running 25 minutes with no preheat uses 0.5 kWh, costing about 19 cent at 38 cent per unit — a few cent more than a higher-wattage machine's shorter cook, because the extra time roughly cancels the lower draw. Compare that to the oven's 2.08 kWh and 79 cent for the same tray bake, and the budget machine still saves around 60 cent per meal, slightly more than a premium one saves, because its lower wattage partly offsets its longer cook time. Across five dinners a week that's close to €15 a month, on a machine that might have cost €35. The energy case for switching from oven to air fryer doesn't depend on spending more; it depends on switching at all.

#### What warranty do you actually get on an air fryer under €100 in Ireland?
At this price point the statutory two-year EU manufacturer guarantee applies exactly the same as it does on a €200 machine, but enforcing it is harder if the seller has no Irish or EU presence. Check the returns address before buying, not after something breaks — a machine sold through a marketplace listing with a UK or non-EU fulfilment address can mean paying return postage and customs charges that exceed the appliance's value. Irish and EU-based retailers such as Currys, Harvey Norman, DID, Argos and Amazon.ie's own stock carry straightforward two-year cover and a local returns process. Where budget machines specifically go wrong on warranty is third-party marketplace sellers using generic Chinese factory listings with no Irish contact; the appliance itself may be identical, but the paperwork behind it isn't.

#### What to never compromise on, even at the lowest price
Three things are worth holding firm on regardless of budget. Basket depth needs to be enough to hold a single layer of a full bag of frozen chips without stacking — check the litre figure against basket photos, not the number alone. Stated wattage needs to be a specific figure, not a range or an 'up to' claim, since that vagueness usually hides a machine that runs cooler and slower than its class average. And the coating needs to be explicitly stated as PFOA-free, which is now standard but occasionally missing from very cheap unbranded listings, worth a direct check rather than an assumption. Digital display, presets and a see-through window are all genuinely nice to have and genuinely optional; none of them affects whether the food comes out right.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Is a €30-40 air fryer worth buying at all?
A: For occasional use — a few times a week, single portions, nothing elaborate — yes, and the crisping performance at this price is closer to a €90 machine than most people expect, because the core mechanism, a fan over a perforated basket, is simple and cheap to get right. What you give up is convenience: a dial timer instead of presets, no shake reminder, and a smaller basket that suits one or two portions rather than a family meal. For daily cooking for a household of three or more, the lack of a shake reminder becomes a genuine daily annoyance rather than a minor one, which is where paying closer to €80-90 starts to earn its keep.

Q: What's the real difference between a €40 and a €90 air fryer?
A: Mostly controls and basket size, not fundamental cooking ability. The €90 machine typically adds a digital touchscreen with cooking presets, a shake reminder that pauses the timer, and a basket around 4.2-4.7 litres versus 2-3.5 litres on the cheaper unit. Wattage usually rises too, from around 1200W to 1700W, shaving a few minutes off cook times. What doesn't reliably improve is the coating quality or how evenly the food browns — both come down to basket shape and fan placement, which vary independently of price. If capacity and convenience don't matter to you, the cooking result itself won't justify the jump.

Q: Do budget air fryers use more electricity to compensate for lower power?
A: Not in any way that costs you money overall. A lower-wattage machine draws less power but takes proportionally longer to cook the same food, so the total energy used, and the bill, work out close to identical either way — often within a few cent per meal. Where budget machines can lose slightly is holding heat less efficiently if the housing is thinner, meaning marginally more energy escapes rather than cooking the food, but the difference is small next to the far larger gap between any air fryer and an oven. Wattage on the spec sheet is a poor proxy for running cost; total kWh per typical cook is the number that actually matters.

Q: Are budget air fryer baskets safe — coatings, PFOA and so on?
A: Generally yes. PFOA-free non-stick coating has been the industry standard for years now, including on unbranded budget listings, and Irish and EU retailers require CE marking regardless of price. The genuine risk at the cheap end isn't the coating chemistry, it's coating durability — thinner, cheaper non-stick layers scratch and degrade faster under metal utensils or abrasive scrubbing, and a damaged coating is more of a cooking-quality issue than a safety one once flaking becomes visible. Use silicone or wooden utensils, avoid scouring pads, and a €35 basket will hold its coating almost as long as a premium one.

Q: How do I know if a cheap air fryer will still be sold in a year for spares?
A: Check whether the manufacturer or an Irish retailer lists a replacement basket or drawer as a separate purchase — if a spare part exists on Amazon.ie or the brand's own site, the model has enough sales volume to justify continued stock. Unbranded or one-off marketplace listings rarely have this, meaning a broken handle or worn-out basket ends the machine's life entirely rather than costing a €15 part. This matters more for budget machines specifically because their lower build quality means something is more likely to need replacing within the first two years, right when spares availability makes the biggest financial difference.

Q: Is it worth waiting for a sale rather than buying a budget model at full price?
A: Usually, yes — budget air fryers see frequent discounting around Black Friday, January sales and mid-year clearance events, often 20-30% off, more than most kitchen appliances. Since the difference between models in this bracket is mostly convenience features rather than cooking ability, waiting a few weeks for a discount on a slightly better-specced machine, digital controls instead of a dial, a larger basket, usually beats buying the cheapest option immediately at full price. The exception is when an existing appliance has just failed and going without isn't practical — in that case, any machine passing the three durability checks is worth buying at full price rather than waiting.

#### What does ‘dual zone’ actually mean on an air fryer?
True dual-zone means two separate heating elements and two separate fans, one per drawer, each running its own temperature and timer — letting one side finish chips at 200°C while the other reheats gravy at 100°C. Cheaper 'dual basket' machines share a single element and fan pushed through a divided housing, so both sides are locked to the same temperature and time regardless of what's cooking in each. The spec sheet rarely states this plainly; look for the word 'independent' next to the zone controls, or check whether the two baskets have separate digital displays versus one shared display toggling between them. A shared-element machine still lets you cook two different foods, just not at genuinely different settings, which matters most for combinations like chips and fish that need different temperatures.

#### Should both air fryer zones be the same size?
Zone sizes on the market split roughly two ways: symmetric, two equal baskets around 3.8-4.5 litres each, or asymmetric, one larger zone paired with a smaller one. Symmetric suits households that regularly cook two similar-sized portions of different things — two proteins, or a main and a substantial side. Asymmetric suits the more common real pattern of one large component, chips or roast vegetables, needing more room than the smaller protein or sauce alongside it. Add the two zones together and compare that combined figure to a single-basket machine's stated capacity; a 3.8+3.8 dual-zone at 7.6 litres combined holds a similar total volume to a single 7-8 litre basket, so the decision is really about needing two independently controlled compartments, not extra overall room. Basket depth is worth checking alongside litres too, since a shallower zone struggles with anything tall, a whole fish fillet or a stack of wings, regardless of its stated volume.

#### The energy case for dual-zone over the oven
A dual-zone machine running both baskets simultaneously at a combined 1.7-2kW for 25 minutes uses roughly 0.7-0.85 kWh, costing 27-32 cent at 38 cent per unit — still a clear win against an oven doing the equivalent two-dish meal, which needs the same 2.08 kWh and 79 cent regardless of how many dishes share the preheat. What dual-zone doesn't meaningfully save is energy compared with cooking the same two items sequentially in a single-basket air fryer, since total wattage-minutes end up similar either way; the real saving there is time, not electricity. Where dual-zone earns a genuine energy advantage is against running two separate single-basket air fryers side by side, which duplicates the standby draw and, on some models, the preheat cycle. That standby-and-preheat duplication is the real argument for choosing one dual-zone machine over two separate single-basket units bought to solve the same two-dish problem, on top of the obvious counter-space saving.

#### Match and sync features: real convenience or a gimmick
The synchronised-finish feature, branded Match Cook, Smart Finish or similar depending on the manufacturer, calculates the cook time difference between two different foods and delays the start of the faster one automatically so both land on the table together. This is the feature actually worth paying for, because manually staggering two timers to hit the same finish point is fiddly enough that most people just don't bother and end up eating in shifts instead. It only works, though, on machines with genuinely independent zone control; a shared-element dual basket can't offer it because both sides are locked to one clock regardless. Check for the specific feature name in the spec sheet rather than assuming any two-drawer machine includes it. Some machines extend the same logic to a full multi-stage sequence — starting a slow reheat, then kicking a second item into a high-heat finish automatically — which is worth checking for if your household regularly cooks more than two components in one sitting.

#### What breaks the two-zone promise
The most common disappointment with dual-zone machines isn't the cooking, it's discovering after purchase that the two zones aren't independently controlled the way the box implied. Read the spec sheet for explicit language — 'two independent cooking zones' or 'individually controlled' — rather than photos of two baskets, which say nothing about the electronics underneath. A second failure mode is combined wattage: two genuinely independent 900W elements running together draw close to 1800W, which is fine on a standard Irish 13A socket but worth checking against anything else plugged into the same circuit, particularly older kitchens with fewer dedicated sockets. The final check is whether both baskets are the same depth — asymmetric length is common and useful, asymmetric depth usually means one side can't fit a standard portion properly.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: What's the difference between dual-zone and two separate baskets in one housing?
A: Genuine dual-zone means two independent heating elements and fans, each with its own temperature and timer, so one side can roast at 200°C while the other holds food warm at 80°C. A cheaper divided-basket machine shares a single element and fan across both compartments, meaning the two sides always run the same temperature and time even though they look identical from the outside. The only reliable way to tell them apart before buying is the spec sheet wording — look for 'independent' zones and two separate digital displays rather than one shared control panel. Photos of two baskets prove nothing about what's happening underneath them.

Q: Does cooking two zones at once use double the electricity?
A: Roughly, yes, since you're running two heating elements simultaneously rather than one — a combined 1.7-2kW draw is normal for genuine dual-zone machines running both sides. But that's still measured against cooking two separate dishes, which would otherwise mean two separate cooking cycles or an oven handling both at once. Compared to an oven cooking the same two-dish meal, dual-zone still costs roughly a third of the price per meal, around 30 cent versus 79 cent, because the oven's fixed preheat energy doesn't scale down for a smaller portion the way an air fryer's shorter, preheat-free cycle does.

Q: Can I run just one zone and leave the other switched off?
A: Yes, on every genuine dual-zone machine — each side operates completely independently, so running a single basket for a smaller meal draws roughly half the combined wattage and costs proportionally less, similar to running a smaller single-basket machine. This matters for households whose portion needs vary night to night; there's no efficiency penalty for using only one side, and no need to fill the second basket just because it's there. Some machines display a slightly higher standby draw with both zones powered even when one basket is empty and idle, but the difference is negligible against the cost of actually running an element.

Q: What is the Match Cook or Sync Finish feature, and is it worth it?
A: It's a setting that calculates the time difference between two different foods cooking in each zone and automatically delays the start of the quicker one, so both finish together rather than one item sitting and cooling while the other catches up. It solves a genuinely annoying manual problem — staggering two separate timers correctly is fiddly enough that most people skip it and just eat in shifts. It's worth prioritising specifically if you regularly cook a main and side with different cook times, chips and fish, for example; if you mostly cook two portions of the same thing, the feature adds little since both zones would finish together anyway.

Q: Is dual-zone worth it for a two-person household?
A: Marginally, and mostly for variety rather than necessity — a well-sized single-zone basket in the 4.5-5.5 litre range already handles two portions of most meals in one load. Dual-zone earns its price for two people specifically when meals regularly involve two different foods needing different settings, one person eating fish while the other has chicken, say, rather than two portions of the same dish. If most dinners are identical portions of one meal, a single-zone machine at a lower price does the same job; the synchronised-finish feature has nothing to synchronise when both sides are cooking the same thing anyway.

Q: Which foods actually benefit most from dual-zone cooking?
A: Combinations needing genuinely different temperatures or times get the clearest benefit — chips at a high, dry heat alongside fish or sausages that want a lower, gentler setting, or a protein finishing while vegetables that cook faster hold warm in the second zone. Reheating pairs well too, warming a side in one zone while the other cooks something fresh. Where dual-zone adds least is two portions of an identical dish, since a single larger basket does that in one load without needing independent settings at all. The feature earns its keep on temperature or timing mismatches, not simply on cooking more than one thing.

#### Does a bigger litre number mean a bigger air fryer basket?
Not necessarily. A single-drawer machine stated at 9–10 litres and a dual-basket machine stated at 10.4 litres combined — two baskets of 5.2 litres each — sound equivalent on paper but behave very differently: the single large drum takes a whole chicken or a full tray of vegetables in one continuous space, while the split machine's two smaller compartments often won't fit a chicken over roughly 1.6kg in either basket. Basket diameter, not total volume, is what determines whether a whole joint or a full family-sized tray fits, and manufacturers rarely publish it. Check product photos for a chicken, a pizza, or a comparable reference object shown inside the actual basket before trusting the litre number on its own.

#### How much time does cooking in two rounds actually cost you?
For a household of five needing roughly five generous portions of chips, a machine with genuine single-layer capacity for three to four adult portions forces a second round, adding 15-20 minutes and meaning the first batch sits cooling, and softening, while the second finishes. A properly sized 9L-plus single drum or a well-matched dual-zone combination avoids this by fitting the full family portion in one pass. The practical Irish comparison is a family of five's typical dinner: a full 900g-1kg bag of frozen chips plus a tray of chicken pieces needs close to 9-10 litres of genuine single-layer basket space to cook in one round without stacking, which is roughly where 'family size' claims on smaller machines start failing the real test. That second round isn't just slower, it also means the reheated first batch loses the crispness that's the entire reason for choosing an air fryer over a microwave in the first place, undermining the appliance's main selling point on the nights it matters most.

#### Energy cost for a family of five: air fryer versus oven, per week
A family cooking a full dinner in the oven most nights, 2.5kW for 50 minutes including preheat, spends about 79 cent in electricity per meal, or roughly €5.50 across seven dinners a week. A large air fryer at 1.8kW for a slightly longer 25-30 minutes needed for a bigger load, no preheat, uses about 0.83 kWh per meal, costing 32 cent — a saving near 47 cent per dinner, or about €3.30 a week, roughly €14 a month. That's smaller in percentage terms than the saving on single-portion cooking, because bigger loads narrow the wattage gap between the two appliances, but it compounds daily for a family cooking dinner every night rather than occasionally, and it comes without sacrificing the one-round capacity a big household actually needs. Scale that saving to a full year of nightly cooking and it lands close to €170, roughly the price difference between a mid-range and a genuinely large-capacity machine, which is one way to think about whether the bigger unit pays for itself.

#### Multi-cooker features worth having at family size
At 9 litres and up, several machines add a rotisserie spit for whole chicken, dedicated baking pans, and multiple wire racks for layered cooking, and these are worth evaluating on genuine usefulness rather than spec-sheet length. A rotisserie function is worth having specifically if whole chicken is a regular family meal, since it produces noticeably more even results than resting the bird flat in a basket. Extra racks matter less than they sound, since stacking two layers in a single chamber usually means the top layer shields the bottom from the fan, undermining the even-cooking case for buying an air fryer in the first place. A dehydrate setting is a genuine bonus for family snack prep but rarely decides a purchase on its own. Check the rotisserie's maximum bird weight against what your family actually buys — many spits cap out around 1.8-2kg, which rules out a larger Sunday roasting chicken even on a machine otherwise sized for family cooking.

#### What a 15L multi-cooker gives up compared to two mid-size machines
Single-chamber machines above 12-15 litres market themselves as oven replacements, but heating a much larger volume of air with one fan and element takes measurably longer to reach temperature than the marketing's 'no preheat' claim implies for smaller machines, even if there's technically no separate preheat step. Space furthest from the fan, typically the bottom corners of a tall chamber, runs measurably cooler, so even cooking across a full family-sized load in one of these units depends more on food placement than in a smaller, more uniformly circulated basket. Families choosing between one large multi-cooker and two separate mid-size machines should weigh counter space and cost against this: two 8L machines cooking simultaneously often finish faster and more evenly than one 15L chamber cooking the same total volume. Two smaller machines also give a family the option to run one now and one later rather than committing the entire meal to a single chamber and a single timer.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Will a large air fryer actually fit a whole chicken?
A: Depends on basket diameter, not the litre figure. A single-drum machine rated 9-10 litres generally fits a whole chicken up to around 1.8-2kg, since the chamber is one continuous space wide enough for the bird's shoulders. A dual-basket machine with the same combined litre rating often won't, because each individual basket is narrower — a chicken that doesn't fit through the opening of a 5.2-litre single drawer won't cook in it regardless of the combined total. If whole chicken is a regular family meal, prioritise single-chamber capacity and check the manufacturer's maximum stated weight for whole poultry specifically, not the general litre figure.

Q: Is a single big drum better than dual-zone for a family of five?
A: For genuinely large single items, whole chicken, a full tray of roast vegetables, a big drum wins on raw capacity. For the more common family pattern of cooking two different things at once, chips and chicken pieces, say, dual-zone wins because both zones run independently rather than needing everything to share one chamber and one setting. Many large families end up better served by a big dual-zone unit, roughly 7.5-9 litres combined, than either a smaller single drum or a smaller dual-zone, since it covers both the single-large-item case reasonably well and the two-different-dishes case properly.

Q: How many portions does a 9-10 litre air fryer actually hold, not on paper?
A: Realistically four to five adult portions of a mixed meal, chips plus a protein, in a single layer without stacking, which is the actual test of whether a machine cooks evenly rather than just holding more food. Manufacturer photos sometimes show more food than that fitted in, but usually stacked, which undermines the airflow the whole appliance depends on. If your household regularly needs six or more portions in one pass, plan on either a genuinely larger single-drum unit above 10 litres or splitting the meal across two machines rather than trusting a single unit's top-line litre claim.

Q: Do big air fryers use noticeably more electricity than small ones?
A: Somewhat, both in wattage and in slightly longer cook times for the larger loads they're built to hold, but the gap is smaller than most people expect. A large 1.8kW machine cooking a big family portion for 25-30 minutes uses around 0.75-0.9 kWh per meal; a small 1.4kW machine cooking a two-person portion for 20 minutes uses about 0.47 kWh. Per portion cooked, the large machine is actually more efficient, since it's spreading a similar preheat-free overhead across more food. The comparison that actually matters isn't large versus small air fryer, it's any air fryer versus the oven it's replacing.

Q: Can a large air fryer completely replace the oven for a big family?
A: For most weeknight dinners, yes, provided the basket genuinely holds a full family portion in one pass rather than forcing rounds. Where it still struggles is baking that needs oven-specific geometry, a large lasagne dish, a full-size cake, bread — and very large roasting joints beyond what any air fryer chamber accommodates, typically anything over about 2.5-3kg. Most large families that make the switch keep the oven specifically for Sunday roasts, baking and big-batch cooking for gatherings, while putting the air fryer to work the other six nights, which is where most of the weekly electricity saving actually piles up.

Q: Is it worth buying a 15L multi-cooker instead of a dedicated oven?
A: Not as a full replacement for most families — a 15L chamber heats less evenly than a proper oven's insulated cavity and airflow design, particularly in the corners furthest from the fan, and it can't match an oven's volume for a large gathering or a full baking tray. It's worth buying alongside an existing oven specifically as the daily-use appliance, faster, cheaper per meal, no preheat, while the oven stays for the jobs that need real volume or steady ambient heat. Treating a multi-cooker as the household's only cooking appliance usually means compromising on the meals that need genuine oven capacity.

Two drawers inevitably mean a wider footprint than the single-basket compacts this page is built around, so it's the choice for someone who wants dual-zone cooking and is willing to give up counter space to get it — the opposite trade-off from our €20 Midea pick.

#### How much counter space does a compact air fryer actually need?
Litre capacity says nothing about counter footprint. A 4-litre compact machine typically measures around 30x30cm at the base, while an 8-litre family machine can run 35x40cm or more, and most air fryers need a further 10–15cm of clearance behind for hot air venting out the back or top. Footprint is the number that actually matters in a Dublin or Cork apartment kitchen, where the usable counter run between sink and hob is often 60–90cm and already shared with a kettle, toaster and microwave — the difference between those two sizes decides whether the machine lives permanently on the counter or gets lifted in and out of a press daily. Pushed flush against a wall or under a cabinet, that exhaust has nowhere to go, which measurably slows cooking and shortens the appliance's working life.

#### How small can an air fryer basket be before it stops being useful?
Two litres suits a single person cooking one real portion at a time, roughly enough for a chicken breast and a modest side, but it's tight for anything requiring a single layer, a full bag of chips barely fits without stacking. Four litres is the practical minimum for genuine flexibility — enough for two smaller portions or one generous one, still compact enough for a narrow counter. Below two litres, several manual dial models exist mainly for reheating and small snacks rather than full meals, which is a legitimate use case if that's genuinely all the appliance needs to do. The honest question before buying compact isn't the smallest available, it's the smallest basket that still fits what you'd actually cook in it without constant compromise. Basket shape matters as much as the litre figure at this size too — a shallow, wide 2-litre basket often cooks more evenly than a deep, narrow one of the same stated volume, since the smaller fan still needs room to circulate air around the food.

#### Heat and steam output in a small room
Air fryers vent hot, moist air continuously while running, typically from vents on the back or top, and in a well-ventilated kitchen that's a non-issue. Many newer Irish apartment builds, though, have compact galley kitchens with limited or no extraction beyond a small integrated fan, and running an air fryer for 20-25 minutes in one of these raises both ambient temperature and humidity noticeably, particularly in summer or in a kitchen without an openable window. This isn't a safety issue, but it's a comfort one worth factoring in before buying, since it affects daily usability more than any spec on the box. Cracking a window or running an extractor fan during cooking largely solves it; positioning the machine away from the room's least-ventilated corner helps more than any product feature can.

#### The cost-per-meal case for one or two people
A single portion cooked in a compact air fryer at 1.3-1.5kW for 15-18 minutes uses roughly 0.35-0.45 kWh, costing 13-17 cent at 38 cent per unit — genuinely cheap, and notably cheaper than the same portion in a larger family-size machine, since smaller loads in a compact unit's tighter chamber circulate and cook slightly faster. Compare that to an oven cooking a single portion, which still needs the full 10-minute preheat regardless of how little food is going in, pushing the cost to around 60-70 cent for a meal a fraction the size of what justifies that preheat. For someone living alone and cooking most nights, that gap adds up to real money — the oven becomes proportionally more wasteful the smaller the portion, which makes a compact air fryer's case strongest exactly where family-size comparisons matter least.

#### What should you check before buying an air fryer you'll store away?
Beyond footprint while running, consider what the machine does when it isn't — several compact models are designed with flat, stackable bases and recessed cords specifically so they store in a press without needing an awkward gap on either side. Weight matters more than it seems for anyone lifting the machine in and out of storage daily rather than leaving it permanently on the counter; compact machines typically run 3-5kg against 6-8kg for family-size units, a real difference for a daily lift from a low cupboard. A carry handle built into the housing, rather than relying on the basket handle, is a small detail that matters disproportionately once the appliance becomes a daily-storage item rather than a permanent counter fixture. Cord length is worth checking too if the machine lives in a press near a single wall socket shared with a kettle or toaster, since a short integrated cord can mean it only reaches the counter from one specific spot.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: What's the smallest air fryer basket size that's still practical for one person?
A: Around 2-2.5 litres covers a genuine single portion, a chicken breast or a few sausages plus a modest side, without constant stacking. Going smaller than that shifts the appliance from a meal-cooking tool into something closer to a snack reheater, fine if that's genuinely the use case, frustrating if you expect to cook proper dinners in it. If counter space allows even a small amount of flexibility, 3.5-4 litres is worth the extra footprint, since it comfortably handles a single generous portion or two smaller ones without feeling like a compromise on every single cook.

Q: Will a compact air fryer fit under a standard kitchen wall unit?
A: Usually, but check the vertical clearance specifically rather than assuming — most compact machines stand 25-30cm tall, and Irish kitchen wall units are typically fitted with 45-55cm of clearance to the counter, so there's normally room, but a taller digital-display model can run closer to 35cm and get tight. The bigger issue isn't height, it's the hot air venting from the top or back on many models, which needs genuine clearance rather than just physical fit — running a machine hard against the underside of a cabinet, even with room to spare, traps heat and can discolour the cabinet base over time.

Q: Is it worth buying a bigger air fryer 'just in case' even in a small kitchen?
A: Generally no, if the kitchen genuinely can't accommodate the footprint day to day — an appliance too large to leave permanently on the counter tends to get used less often, not more, because lifting a heavy 8-litre machine out of a low press for a single portion is enough friction that people default back to the microwave or oven instead. Buying to the kitchen's actual constraint, and accepting occasional double-batching for larger meals, generally produces more real-world use than buying capacity that then sits unused in storage. The exception is genuinely expecting a household size increase soon — a partner moving in, a baby on the way — where sizing up ahead of the need makes sense.

Q: Do compact air fryers make more noise or heat than larger ones?
A: Noise is roughly comparable across sizes, since it's driven mainly by fan speed rather than chamber volume, though a smaller sealed housing can make the fan sound slightly more noticeable in a quiet room. Heat output while running is lower in absolute terms, since compact machines draw less wattage, but it's more concentrated in a smaller kitchen footprint, which is why ventilation matters more for compact machines in small rooms than the raw wattage figure suggests. Neither factor should be a deciding one on its own; basket capacity and counter footprint matter far more for a compact-kitchen decision than the modest differences in noise or heat.

Q: Can I store a compact air fryer in a cupboard between uses?
A: Yes, provided it's fully cooled first — most manufacturer guidance recommends 20-30 minutes after switching off before packing it away, since residual heat in an enclosed press with no airflow can affect nearby items and, over repeated cycles, the appliance's own plastic housing. Check the model's weight and whether it has a proper carry handle if this is a daily routine rather than occasional; compact machines built specifically for small kitchens tend to include this, while family-size machines rebadged as 'compact' sometimes don't, which becomes obvious the first time you actually lift one out of a low cupboard.

Q: Is cooking for one person in an air fryer actually cheaper than a microwave meal?
A: In electricity terms, an air fryer costs more per cook than a microwave, roughly 13-17 cent against 3-5 cent for a similar reheating job, since microwaves are dramatically more efficient at moving energy directly into food. Where the air fryer wins is food cost and quality for meals a microwave can't produce properly, fresh chicken, chips, roasted vegetables, versus a pre-packaged ready meal, which typically costs several euro more than the same ingredients cooked from raw. For genuine reheating of an existing meal, the microwave wins outright on cost; for cooking a meal from raw ingredients for one, the air fryer usually wins on total cost once food price is included.

# CATEGORY: Air Purifiers
URL: https://pickireland.best/air-purifiers/
5 guides, 30 product entries
==============================================================================

Irish homes have an indoor air problem nobody talks about: damp-driven mould spores, dust mites thriving in humidity, pollen seasons that now run March to September, and solid-fuel smoke drifting through winter estates. A true HEPA purifier removes 99.95%+ of these particles. We compare real performance — CADR, filter costs, noise — across every budget.

## HEPA means H13 or it doesn't mean much
Look for 'True HEPA' H13/H14 — filters capturing 99.95%+ of 0.3-micron particles. 'HEPA-type' or 'HEPA-like' is marketing for lesser filters. For Irish mould spores (1–20 microns) and pollen (10–100 microns), genuine H13 catches essentially everything.

## CADR is the horsepower figure
Clean Air Delivery Rate tells you how much purified air the unit moves. Match it to your room: you want the room's volume cleaned 3–5 times per hour. A typical 20 m² Irish living room (~50 m³) needs a CADR of 150–250 m³/h minimum.

## Filter costs are the real price
A €150 purifier with €60 annual filters costs more over five years than a €250 unit with €30 filters. We factor replacement costs into every recommendation — it's where cheap brands claw their money back.

## Placement and runtime
Run continuously on low/auto rather than blasting occasionally — particle levels rebound within hours. Place 30+ cm from walls, ideally in the room you sleep in: you spend a third of your life there breathing its air.

Full running-cost table for every air purifier we track: https://pickireland.best/air-purifiers/air-purifier-running-costs-ireland.html

#### What are Irish air purifiers actually filtering out?
Irish indoor air is dominated by year-round mould spores (2–10 microns) from persistent humidity, large grass pollen (20–35 microns) that any decent filter traps easily, and sub-micron combustion particles from open fires and stoves that no fibre filter touches alone. That mix calls for a true H13 filter rated to 0.3 microns plus genuine activated carbon measured by weight, not a thin mesh sheet. The particle mix in an Irish house is not the continental one the marketing is written for, and combustion is the awkward fraction: smoke from open fires, ranges and stoves across older estates produces PM2.5 and PM1 particles well under a micron, plus gases that no fibre filter touches at all. A unit optimised purely for pollen will underperform badly on a still winter evening.

#### How do you read an air purifier's CADR and room-size claim?
Coverage claims on the box — "cleans 90 m²" — are usually calculated at one air change per hour on maximum fan speed. One air change is close to useless; three to five is the target. Work from the CADR figure in cubic metres per hour instead and divide it by your room volume. A 250 m³/h unit in a 20 m² sitting room with 2.4 m ceilings, so 48 m³, delivers about five changes an hour, which is genuinely good. The same unit in a 45 m² open-plan space of 108 m³ manages barely two. Check which speed the CADR was measured at, too, because top speed on most machines is unusable in an occupied room. If a listing quotes only square metres and never gives a m³/h figure, the omission is the answer.

#### What does an air purifier really cost over five years?
Price the machine over five years, not at the checkout. Take a €200 mid-range unit with a €45 combined HEPA-and-carbon filter replaced annually: that is €225 in consumables. Electricity is larger than most people assume — 20 W running continuously is 175 kWh a year, which at Irish standard rates of roughly 38 cent a unit comes to about €67 a year, or €333 across five years. Running total: €758. Now take a €110 budget unit whose only filter costs €55 and is rated for six months: €550 of filters over the same period, usually with a less efficient motor as well. The cheaper box wins at the till and loses everywhere afterwards. Check the replacement filter's current price and Irish stock before buying the machine; that one search prevents most of the regret.

#### Which air purifier certifications actually mean something?
Three marks are worth looking for here. AHAM Verifide means the CADR figures were measured to a common test standard rather than self-declared. The ECARF seal and the Allergy UK Seal of Approval indicate that someone other than the manufacturer assessed allergen reduction — imperfect, but better than a brand's own bar chart. EN 1822 or ISO 29463 classification, the source of the H13 and H14 grades, tells you the media itself was tested, though it says nothing about whether the housing leaks around it. Gasketed, sealed filter chambers matter more than the grade on the sticker: air takes the easiest path, and on cheaply moulded bodies that path runs around the filter rather than through it. Absent all of these, ask whether the brand publishes a m³/h CADR and a dB(A) figure at a stated distance.

#### Buying in Ireland: filters, warranty and support
Physical retail for purifiers is thin here, so most purchases happen online through Amazon.ie, Currys, Harvey Norman, DID or a brand's own store. Two practical consequences follow. First, confirm the replacement filter has an Irish or EU fulfilment route; owner reports consistently mention long waits and unexpected customs charges on filters shipped from outside the EU, which quietly doubles their cost. Second, check the warranty is honoured by an EU entity, because posting a six-kilo appliance to a UK service address is rarely worth the trouble. Third-party filters exist for popular models at roughly half price, but some machines carry an RFID chip that refuses to reset the filter counter for a non-genuine part. That is not a dealbreaker, just a cost worth pricing in before the box is sitting in your hall.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Which room should I put my first air purifier in?
A: The bedroom, in almost every case. You spend seven to nine hours a night in there with the door closed, which is both the longest continuous exposure of your day and by far the easiest volume for a purifier to actually clean — a sealed 12 m² room is a fair fight, an open-plan downstairs is not. A sitting room is the second choice if you have an open fire or a stove, or if someone in the house is home all day. Only add a second unit once the first is running continuously and you have judged whether it made a difference.

Q: Do I need to run an air purifier all year in Ireland, or just in pollen season?
A: All year suits most Irish homes, because the triggers rotate rather than stop. Tree and grass pollen run from February through July, weed pollen and outdoor mould spores carry into September, and the damp months that follow bring indoor spores and solid-fuel smoke drifting from neighbouring chimneys. There is no genuinely clean month. Running continuously on a low or auto setting costs a few euro a month and stops particle levels rebounding, which they do within a couple of hours of the unit being switched off. Seasonal-only use makes sense if you have a single confirmed trigger and nothing else.

Q: Can an air purifier replace opening the windows?
A: No, and they solve different problems. A purifier recirculates and filters air already in the room; it removes particles but does nothing about carbon dioxide, cooking moisture or the stale feel of an unventilated space. Irish homes, especially well-sealed newer builds, need ventilation to control humidity — and humidity control is what actually prevents mould forming in the first place. The workable compromise during pollen season is to ventilate briefly in the middle of the day or just after rain, when grass counts are lower, then close up and let the purifier deal with what came in.

Q: Do air purifiers remove radon or carbon monoxide?
A: No. Radon is a radioactive gas and a real concern in parts of Ireland — the EPA publishes high-radon maps covering large areas of the west, midlands and southeast — but it is a gas, and HEPA media only captures particles. Activated carbon does not hold it either. Radon is dealt with through testing, sub-floor sumps and ventilation. Carbon monoxide is the same story: no domestic purifier removes it, and none is any substitute for a working CO alarm. If a listing claims otherwise, that alone tells you what the brand's other claims are worth.

Q: How long does an air purifier take to clean a room?
A: Roughly the time needed for three to four air changes, so with a correctly sized unit you are looking at 30 to 60 minutes from a standing start on a medium speed. The arithmetic is simple: divide the CADR in m³/h by the room volume to get changes per hour. A 200 m³/h machine in a 48 m³ sitting room manages about four an hour, so most of the improvement lands inside the first twenty minutes. The catch is that particles keep arriving from outside and from ordinary activity, which is why continuous low-speed running beats occasional blasts on turbo.

Q: Are third-party replacement filters worth buying?
A: Often, with two caveats. Generic filters for popular models typically cost 40–60% less, and the better ones use genuine H13 media, but there is no way to verify the grade from a listing photograph — buy from sellers with a long review history and check that the pleat count and depth match the original. The second issue is chipped filters: some manufacturers embed an RFID tag so the machine will not reset its counter for a non-genuine part. You can generally still run it, but the reminder light stays on. Factor that in when choosing the machine, not afterwards.

#### When does hay fever season actually run in Ireland?
Irish allergy season is really three overlapping ones: hazel and alder from February, birch and ash from March to May, and grass — the main hay-fever trigger — from mid-May through July, peaking around mid-June. Met Éireann publishes a daily pollen forecast from 1 February to 30 September, the practical window for keeping windows shut and a purifier running. Weed pollen and outdoor mould spores then carry the load into September, especially after warm damp spells. If you react only in June you can run the machine seasonally, but most Irish sufferers are sensitised to more than one trigger and do better leaving it on from early spring, with auto mode throttling it back on quiet days.

#### Why the bedroom beats the sitting room
The highest-value place for an allergy purifier is beside the bed. You spend seven to nine unbroken hours there with the door shut, and that is the only stretch of the day when the machine works on a small, sealed volume without fresh pollen walking in on clothes and hair. A 12 m² bedroom with a 2.4 m ceiling is about 29 m³, so a modest 120 m³/h CADR gives four air changes an hour — comfortably enough. The routine matters as much as the hardware: close the window by late afternoon, when grass pollen settles back to ground level on a warm evening, shower and wash your hair before bed, and keep the day's clothes out of the room. The purifier then handles what remains airborne instead of fighting a constant inflow.

#### Why won't a HEPA filter fix a dust mite problem?
House dust mites thrive in Irish humidity, and their allergen — a protein carried in their droppings — is a common year-round trigger. But that allergen mostly rides on heavy particles which settle within minutes of being disturbed, so it spends very little time suspended. A purifier catches what gets stirred up during bed-making and hoovering; it cannot pull allergen out of a mattress or a carpet. If mites are your diagnosis, the machine is a supporting player behind allergen-proof mattress and pillow encasements, hot-washing bedding weekly, and keeping indoor relative humidity below 50%. Pet dander is the opposite case entirely: it is light, stays suspended for hours, and is exactly the load HEPA filtration removes well. Match the tool to the allergen rather than buying on the word "allergy" alone.

#### Why does a sealed housing matter more than the filter grade?
An H13 filter only helps if all of the air goes through it. Cheaply moulded bodies without gaskets let a slice of the airflow slip around the media, and for an allergy sufferer that bypass is the difference between relief and nothing. Look for a filter seating against a rubber or foam seal and a door that clamps rather than clips. The pre-filter matters too: grains at 20–35 microns and pet hair clog fine media fast, so a washable mesh pre-filter rinsed monthly through summer adds months to the life of the expensive element behind it. Independent marks — the ECARF seal, the Allergy UK Seal of Approval — at least indicate somebody other than the manufacturer assessed allergen performance. Neither guarantees results, but their absence on a product sold specifically for allergies is worth noticing.

#### What a hay fever season actually costs to run
Run the numbers for a bedroom unit across the Irish season. A machine drawing 8 W on a low overnight setting, eight hours a night from mid-May to the end of August, uses under 8 kWh — around €3 for the entire season at the 38 cent per kWh most Irish standard tariffs charge in 2026. Leave the same unit running 24 hours a day year-round at 15 W and it is 131 kWh, close to €50 a year. Filters are the real expense, and allergy households replace them sooner because pollen and dander load the media faster, so budget €40–70 annually rather than trusting the manufacturer's optimistic twelve months. Set against fifteen weeks of antihistamines and broken sleep that is modest — but compare units on filter price, not sticker price.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Do air purifiers actually stop hay fever symptoms?
A: They reduce indoor exposure rather than cure the allergy. With windows shut and a correctly sized HEPA unit running in the bedroom, indoor pollen levels drop substantially, and the benefit most Irish sufferers describe is better sleep and a milder morning — you start the day without an overnight allergen load already in your system. It does nothing for the hours spent outdoors, commuting or at work, so treat it as one layer alongside antihistamines, nasal sprays and the usual avoidance habits. Anyone with severe or worsening symptoms should be talking to a pharmacist or GP rather than shopping for appliances.

Q: Should I keep bedroom windows closed during grass pollen season?
A: Yes, from mid-May to late July especially, and above all in the early morning and the evening. Grass pollen rises through the morning as the air warms, stays high all afternoon, then sinks back to ground level as things cool — the classic hay fever window on a warm Irish evening. Air the room in the middle of the day, or after rain has washed the air, then close up. A purifier running with the window open during a high count is fighting a losing battle: it can only filter air faster than new pollen arrives, and it will not win that race.

Q: How long before I notice a difference?
A: For the air itself, under an hour. For symptoms, give it two to three weeks of consistent nightly use before judging. Allergic inflammation is cumulative — nasal passages irritated for months do not settle overnight, and one good night is not evidence in either direction. Run it every night with the door closed and the window shut, keep the rest of your routine steady, and compare how you wake across a fortnight. If nothing has shifted after a month of proper use in a correctly sized room, pollen is probably not your main indoor trigger and it is worth looking at mites, damp or pets.

Q: Will a purifier help if the dog or cat sleeps in the bedroom?
A: It will help, but the animal undoes much of the work. Pet dander is light enough to stay suspended for hours, which is precisely what HEPA filtration handles well, and a unit running beside the bed measurably lowers the airborne load. The problem is supply: an animal in the room replenishes dander continuously and deposits it in the bedding you breathe against all night. Keeping the pet out of the bedroom achieves more than any purifier will. If that is not happening, expect faster filter loading and budget for replacement well ahead of the stated interval.

Q: Does an air purifier help with autumn mould spore allergy?
A: Yes, and it is an underrated use here. Outdoor mould spore counts — Alternaria and Cladosporium in particular — climb through late summer and peak around September and October, when mild damp weather follows a warm spell. Those spores sit in the 2–10 micron range and are captured efficiently by H13 media. Indoors, the same filter catches spores released from damp patches and from condensation forming on cold external walls. What it cannot do is stop them being produced: where there is visible mould or persistent condensation, the moisture itself has to be dealt with.

Q: Should the purifier be right beside the bed or across the room?
A: Beside the bed, but not aimed at your face. A metre or two from the pillow puts the clean-air outlet inside your breathing zone, which is where it does most good, and it keeps the controls in reach. Leave 30 cm clear of the wall and the headboard so the intake is not blocked, and angle the outlet along the bed rather than at it — constant airflow on your face is drying, and in an unheated Irish bedroom in February it is cold as well. A low bedside locker is usually the best compromise.

#### What does a 25 dB air purifier actually sound like?
Decibels are logarithmic, so the gap between 25 dB and 35 dB is far wider than it reads — every 10 dB is roughly a doubling of perceived loudness. A quiet Irish bedroom sits around 20-30 dB of background noise at night, so a purifier at 24 dB effectively disappears into it, while one at 38 dB is impossible to ignore at 3am. The catch is measurement. Manufacturer figures are taken in an anechoic chamber at one metre; the same unit on a hard bedside locker 40 cm from your ear, reflecting off a wall, reads higher in practice. Treat quoted sleep-mode numbers as a ranking tool between models rather than a promise. Any figure given without a distance, or as an "as low as" range with no speed named, is not really a specification.

#### Sleep-mode CADR: the number that decides everything
Any purifier can be silent — switch it off. What matters is how much clean air survives the quiet setting. Brands headline maximum CADR at top speed, which on most machines is 50–55 dB and unusable in an occupied bedroom. The useful question is airflow at the lowest setting. A unit delivering 60–80 m³/h below 25 dB turns over a 29 m³ Irish double bedroom two to three times an hour, which is enough to matter. One that drops to 25 m³/h in order to hit its silence claim gives under one change an hour and is essentially decorative. Where brands publish per-speed tables, read them. Where they do not, owner reports consistently mention whether the low setting moves perceptible air at arm's length, and that crude proxy is better than nothing.

#### Why are bigger air purifiers usually the quieter ones?
Noise comes from air velocity and turbulence, not from cleaning. A 360 mm cylindrical unit with a large impeller moves the same volume as a compact tower at a far lower blade speed, and lower blade speed means less broadband hiss. That is why physically larger purifiers tend to be the quiet ones, and why an oversized machine loafing on setting one beats a small one straining on setting three. Motor type matters as well: brushless DC motors run smoother and allow genuinely low speeds, while cheap AC motors have a floor below which they stall or hum. The last variable is tone. Broadband whoosh disappears into sleep; a bearing whine, or a resonance that appears at one particular speed, does not — and it is the most common complaint in long-term owner feedback.

#### Light, draught and the three-in-the-morning problems
Two non-acoustic details ruin bedroom purifiers. The first is light: air-quality LEDs, illuminated rings and bright displays are genuinely disruptive in a dark room, so the unit needs a full display-off mode rather than a dimmed one — a strip of tape is a poor answer on a €300 appliance. The second is auto mode. A purifier left on auto ramps up whenever the sensor sees a spike, and in a bedroom that spike is usually you rolling over and disturbing dust. Waking at three to a machine at full tilt defeats the point, so favour models whose sleep mode locks the fan speed instead of merely dimming the lights. Draught is the third consideration: a directional tower pointed at the bed is unpleasantly cold in an Irish bedroom in January.

#### Overnight running costs and how fast the filter loads
A bedroom-only purifier is cheap to run. At 6 W on sleep mode for eight hours a night, a full year of overnight use is 17.5 kWh — about €7 at current Irish unit rates. Leave the same unit on low around the clock and it is roughly 53 kWh, or €20 a year. Neither figure should change your decision; filters will. Night-only running loads the media far more slowly than continuous operation, so an element rated for twelve months of constant use often stretches well past that on a bedroom duty cycle. Judge replacement by airflow and smell rather than by the counter, which on most machines simply counts hours regardless of load. Budget €30–60 a year and check that price before buying, because small units are where filter mark-ups are steepest.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: How many decibels is too loud for a bedroom?
A: Above about 30 dB most people notice a purifier in a quiet room, and above 35 dB it becomes the loudest thing in there. A typical Irish bedroom at night has a background of 20–30 dB, so anything at or below 25 dB effectively disappears into it. Remember that manufacturer figures are measured at one metre in a treated room; on a hard bedside locker close to your head, add a few decibels in practice. If you are a light sleeper, prioritise models that publish a dB(A) figure for each fan speed over those quoting a single "as low as" number with no context.

Q: Is the white noise from a purifier good for sleep?
A: For some people, genuinely yes — a steady broadband hiss masks traffic, wind and a partner's movement, and plenty of owners keep a unit running mainly for that. What matters is the character of the sound rather than its level. Smooth, low-frequency airflow noise is easy to sleep through; a bearing whine, a motor hum at one particular speed, or a fan that surges up and down on auto is not, and habituation does not fix it. If you want the masking effect, choose a unit that holds a fixed medium speed rather than one that hunts.

Q: Should I use auto mode or sleep mode overnight?
A: Sleep mode, in most bedrooms. Auto reacts to the sensor, and the sensor reacts to ordinary night-time events — turning over, the duvet moving, dust stirred as you get up. The result is a machine ramping to a noisy speed at three in the morning, which is the single most common complaint in long-term owner feedback. A fixed low speed cleans a bedroom-sized volume perfectly well across eight hours. Save auto mode for daytime use in living areas, where a spike from cooking or an opened door is genuinely worth an immediate response.

Q: Can I put the purifier in a corner or under the bed?
A: No to under the bed, and corners are a compromise. Almost all purifiers draw air in through the sides or base and exhaust upwards or forwards, so boxing one in starves the intake, drops actual delivery well below the rated CADR, and makes the motor work harder and louder for less clean air. Aim for 30 cm of clear space around the intake faces, and avoid deep pile carpet if the unit breathes from underneath. Where floor space is tight, a tall slim tower against a wall loses less performance than a cylindrical model jammed into a corner.

Q: Do purifiers make a bedroom colder or draughty?
A: They do not cool the air — the motor actually adds a watt or two of heat — but they move it, and moving air feels colder against skin. In an Irish bedroom in winter, with an external wall sitting at 14–16 °C, an outlet pointed at the bed is noticeably chilly. The fix is placement rather than a different machine: angle the discharge along the room or up towards the ceiling, or choose a cylindrical model with 360-degree output that never concentrates flow in one direction. On sleep mode the airflow is usually too gentle to feel at all.

Q: Do air purifiers get louder as the filter clogs?
A: Usually yes, and it is a useful signal. As media loads with dust, resistance rises, and a fan holding the same speed against more back-pressure gets louder while moving less air. On units with fixed manual speeds you hear it first as a change in tone; on models with automatic pressure compensation you may only see the power draw creep up. Vacuuming or rinsing the pre-filter monthly delays it considerably. If a machine that used to disappear at night is now audible on the same setting, check the pre-filter before assuming the main element is finished.
