#### Why does a robot mower's real coverage fall short of the box figure?
Manufacturer coverage figures are measured under close-to-ideal conditions: flat ground, simple rectangular boundaries, minimal obstacles. Owner reports consistently describe real coverage running 15–30% below the headline figure once a garden has meaningful complexity, so treat the advertised number as a ceiling and size up rather than buying to the exact figure your lawn measures. A rural Irish site rated at 2,000 m² on the box rarely resembles that test layout — it more often includes a gently sloped field-adjacent lawn, a gravel driveway cutting through the middle, and boundary hedging that eats into usable mowing time as the machine repeatedly re-approaches the edge. This isn't manufacturers overstating specifications so much as test conditions rarely matching a working rural garden, which is why owner reports from comparable sites are more useful than the box copy.

#### Multi-zone gardens: driveways, gates and separate lawns
Large rural and suburban Irish properties are rarely one continuous lawn. A gravel or tarmac driveway splitting the front from the back, a five-bar gate between a garden and an adjoining field-side lawn, or an orchard patch set apart from the main cutting area are all common layouts on gardens over 1,000 m². Multi-zone mapping — supported by most large-capacity models on this list — lets you define each area separately with its own schedule, and either lets the mower cross a connecting strip automatically or requires manual relocation between disconnected zones. Before buying, count how many genuinely separate zones your property has, since a mower's advertised zone limit (commonly 3–5) can be a hard ceiling on some models. It's also worth confirming whether crossing a driveway or gate needs a scheduled window of its own, since some models pause at a zone boundary until conditions — daylight, a closed gate — are met before continuing automatically.

#### Slopes, AWD and rough rural ground
Slope tolerance and ground clearance matter far more at this scale, since large Irish sites are more likely to include an incline, an uneven field margin or rough grass a standard suburban mower was never designed to cross. All-wheel drive models hold traction on wet slopes where two-wheel-drive units can spin out or stall, and a higher ground clearance reduces the chance of scalping on uneven turf or grounding out on ridges. Manufacturer slope ratings (often 35–50% on AWD models) should be checked against the steepest section of your actual lawn, not the average gradient, because a mower that copes fine on a gentle overall slope can still struggle on one steep bank near a boundary. Ground clearance matters alongside traction on rural sites with molehills, uneven field margins or old tree roots breaking the surface, since a low-clearance mower can ground out on terrain a standard suburban lawn would never present.

#### How does battery capacity limit a mower on a big lawn?
Covering 1,000 m² or more means the mower spends a meaningfully larger share of its schedule mowing rather than idle on the dock, so battery capacity and recharge time become practical constraints rather than a spec-sheet detail. A larger battery with a shorter recharge window keeps more of the day available for cutting, which matters most in June and July when Irish grass growth peaks. Running costs stay modest regardless of scale — these are low-wattage electric machines, and even frequent charging across a large multi-zone garden adds only a small amount to a typical household electricity bill compared with fuel for a ride-on mower. Solar-assisted charging exists on some large-capacity models but rarely replaces mains charging entirely in Irish light conditions, so treat it as a modest top-up rather than a way to cut charging time significantly during a large multi-zone schedule.

#### Buried wire or wire-free on a large, irregular garden?
On a large or irregularly shaped property, the choice between a buried wire and wire-free navigation is less about convenience and more about reliability at range. RTK-based wire-free systems need a reasonably clear line to satellite signal, which can degrade under dense tree cover or close to tall boundary hedging common on older rural sites — a factor worth weighing against the labour of burying wire across a long or complex perimeter. Some owners of large, signal-challenged gardens choose a hybrid approach: wire-free for open zones, with a short buried-wire section only around the specific area where satellite accuracy is unreliable. Whichever approach you choose, walk the full perimeter yourself before committing, since a boundary that looks straightforward on a site plan can include a signal-blocking outbuilding or dense hedge line that only becomes obvious on the ground.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: How many charge cycles does a robot mower need to cover a half-acre lawn?
A: A half-acre (roughly 2,000 m²) typically needs several charge cycles per week during peak growth in early summer, dropping to one or two as growth slows in autumn and nearly none in mid-winter. Exact numbers depend on the mower's cutting width and battery capacity, but large-capacity models are built around this pattern, with recharge times generally under two hours so the mower can complete a full multi-zone schedule within daylight hours. Owner reports on larger properties suggest budgeting for daily short sessions during May and June specifically, rather than assuming the same weekly routine holds year-round.

Q: Can a robot mower manage a garden split by a driveway or gate?
A: Yes, provided the model supports multi-zone mapping, which is standard on the large-capacity end of the market. A gravel driveway or a gate can either be crossed automatically, if the mower is rated to cross that surface safely, or treated as a hard boundary between two zones that the mower switches between on schedule, sometimes requiring you to manually move it between disconnected areas. Check the specific crossing capability before buying if your layout depends on the mower moving itself between zones without help, since not every model handles gravel or tarmac crossings the same way.

Q: Is all-wheel drive necessary for a large Irish garden?
A: Not for every large garden, but it's worth prioritising if your lawn includes any noticeable slope, rough or uneven ground, or wet low-lying patches that stay soft after rain. Two-wheel-drive models handle flat, well-drained large lawns without issue and cost less. AWD earns its premium on the kind of mixed rural terrain common outside flat estate developments — a field-adjacent lawn with a bank, or ground that turns soft after a wet week, both being realistic scenarios on Irish rural properties rather than edge cases.

Q: What slope gradient is too steep for a robot mower?
A: Manufacturer maximum slope ratings for large-capacity robot mowers typically range from 35% to 50% (roughly 19–27 degrees) on AWD models, and noticeably lower on two-wheel-drive units. Treat the published figure as the absolute limit under ideal dry, grippy conditions, not a comfortable working gradient — wet grass reduces effective traction significantly, and a slope near the rated maximum is a common cause of the mower getting stuck or aborting a session. If a section of your lawn is close to the stated limit, expect more frequent manual intervention there than on the rest of the garden.

Q: How do manufacturers calculate the coverage figure on the box?
A: The headline coverage figure is generally based on the mower completing its full cutting schedule on a flat, simply-shaped lawn with minimal obstacles, within a set number of charge cycles per week. It doesn't account for the extra time spent re-approaching complex boundaries, navigating multiple zones, or climbing slopes, all of which reduce the effective area a mower can keep up with in practice. Owner reports on gardens with real complexity — hedging, gates, uneven ground — consistently describe usable coverage below the box figure, which is why sizing up for a large or complex Irish property is standard advice rather than caution for its own sake.

#### How do wire-free robot mowers actually know where your lawn ends?
Wire-free robot mowers navigate using one of three core technologies, often combined. RTK (Real-Time Kinematic) GPS uses a base station on your property to correct standard satellite positioning down to centimetre-level accuracy. Camera-based vision systems build a visual map during setup and recognise the boundary and obstacles the way a self-driving car reads a road, which helps in tree-shaded areas where satellite signal weakens. Some budget models use fixed beacons placed around the garden as reference points instead. Higher-end machines combine RTK with camera vision so each system compensates for the other's weak spots — satellite for open ground, cameras for shaded or signal-poor corners. Beacon-based systems are becoming less common as RTK hardware costs fall, but they remain a reasonable budget option for a simple, open garden where centimetre-level precision isn't essential.

#### Setup in an afternoon: what the walk-around process involves
Wire-free setup replaces a day of trenching with an app-guided walk. You carry or push the mower once around the boundary you want it to respect, marking gates, obstacles and any no-go zones as you go, and the app builds a digital map from the RTK or camera data collected during that walk. Multi-zone gardens take longer, since each connected or disconnected area typically needs its own walk-around pass. Most manufacturers recommend doing this walk in good weather with clear satellite visibility for RTK models, since heavy cloud or dense tree cover during the initial mapping can reduce boundary accuracy — a poor first map is the most common cause of a wire-free mower straying near an edge in its first few weeks. It's worth repeating the walk-around a second time if the app flags any low-confidence sections of the boundary, since correcting the map before the first unattended run is far easier than troubleshooting an odd cutting pattern afterwards.

#### Where wire-free struggles: signal, shade and dense boundaries
No wire-free navigation method is immune to interference. RTK accuracy can degrade under dense tree canopy, close to tall stone walls, or in gardens overshadowed by a two-storey extension, since these all block or reflect satellite signal. Camera-based systems, in turn, rely on adequate light and can lose confidence in very low winter light or dense fog, both realistic on Irish winter mornings. In practice this rarely means the mower fails outright — it usually means reduced boundary precision in the affected zone, showing up as the mower cutting slightly short of a hedge line it handles precisely elsewhere in the garden. Gardens with one specific problem area often solve it with a supplementary physical boundary marker in just that section rather than switching systems entirely. None of this is unique to any one brand — it's a physical limitation of satellite and optical positioning generally, so the practical fix is choosing a hybrid system and mapping problem areas carefully rather than expecting a single technology to solve every garden.

#### Changing your garden layout later
The practical advantage of wire-free over buried wire shows up months after installation, when the garden changes. Adding a raised bed, extending a patio, or putting up a new shed means editing a digital boundary in the app — a five-minute change — rather than digging up and relaying a physical cable. This matters more in Ireland than it might elsewhere, since many gardens here are actively developed over their first few years in a new estate: decking added, borders dug, a play area installed as children grow. Families still landscaping their garden get more long-term value from a wire-free system's flexibility than from any single feature comparison at the point of purchase. It also removes the seasonal temptation to simply mow around a new obstacle rather than properly updating the boundary, since editing the map correctly takes barely longer than doing it the sloppy way.

#### Theft and tracking on machines with no wire to steal
A robot mower parked on open grass, sometimes visible from the street, is a realistic theft target regardless of navigation type, and wire-free models don't change that risk on their own. What they typically add is stronger anti-theft software: GPS location tracking that works through the same positioning hardware used for mowing, PIN-code unlock so a stolen unit won't operate without the code, and loud on-board alarms triggered by lifting or moving the mower unexpectedly. When comparing wire-free models for a garden visible from outside the property, check which of these three features are included rather than assuming they come as standard — some budget wire-free models include GPS mapping for cutting but skip theft-specific tracking entirely. Registering the mower's serial number with the manufacturer at purchase is also worth doing immediately, since it's the detail most often missing when an owner tries to report a stolen unit later.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Does wire-free navigation work reliably under trees or near high walls?
A: Reliability drops in these conditions but rarely fails completely on modern hybrid systems. Dense tree canopy and tall stone walls both interfere with satellite signal used by RTK positioning, which can reduce boundary accuracy in that specific area of the garden. Models that combine RTK with camera vision handle this better, since the camera can maintain positioning using visual landmarks when satellite signal weakens. If a significant part of your garden sits under heavy tree cover, prioritise a hybrid navigation model over a pure GPS-RTK one, and expect to check boundary accuracy in that zone specifically after the initial setup walk.

Q: How accurate is RTK GPS compared to a buried wire?
A: A buried wire gives a fixed, unambiguous boundary — the mower simply can't cross it. RTK GPS is typically accurate to within 2–5 cm under good satellite conditions, which is precise enough for almost all garden boundaries in practice, but it's a probabilistic system rather than a physical barrier, so accuracy can drift slightly in poor signal conditions. For most gardens with a reasonably open sky view, the practical difference is negligible; the main scenario where a physical wire still edges out RTK is a boundary running directly alongside a feature — a pond, a drop, a road — where zero margin for error matters more than typical.

Q: What happens if a wire-free mower loses GPS signal mid-cut?
A: Most current models are designed to stop and either wait for signal to return or return to the dock using its last known reliable position, rather than continuing to cut blind. Hybrid RTK-and-camera systems are more resilient here, since the camera can maintain a rough sense of position using visual references even during a brief satellite dropout. A genuine full signal loss is uncommon on modern hardware in typical Irish garden conditions, but it's more likely in a garden with heavy tree cover or close to a large building, which is worth factoring in if your site has either.

Q: Can wire-free mowers share boundaries with a neighbour's garden?
A: Yes — the digital boundary you set in the app can run precisely along a shared fence or wall line, the same way a buried wire would, without needing the neighbour's involvement or access to their side. The advantage over a physical wire is that adjusting the line later, if a fence is replaced or moved slightly, is an app edit rather than a dig. It's worth double-checking boundary accuracy along a shared line during the first few cutting sessions, since this is exactly the kind of edge where a few centimetres of drift is most likely to be noticed by a neighbour.

Q: Can I add a wire-free mower to a garden that already has a buried wire from an old machine?
A: Yes. The new wire-free mower ignores the existing cable entirely — it builds its own map using satellite or camera data during the app walk-around, with no interaction with a buried wire from a previous machine. You can leave the old wire in the ground undisturbed or dig up sections you want to reclaim; there's no functional need to remove it before switching systems. This is a common upgrade path for anyone replacing an older wired mower without wanting to disturb an established lawn to extract the cable.

#### What does a robot mower under €700 actually get you in 2026?
Under €700 now buys a genuine robot mower rather than a compromised toy — both wired and wire-free options exist, typically covering gardens up to 200–500m² with basic app scheduling, rain sensors, and simple bump-based or entry-level camera obstacle detection. What you're generally not getting is multi-zone mapping, all-wheel drive, RTK-grade positioning, or advanced anti-theft tracking, which push a model past €1,000. For a typical sub-300 m² Irish estate garden with a single, reasonably simple boundary, the budget tier covers the actual job competently; the trade-offs matter more as garden complexity or size increases beyond that. It's also worth checking exactly which accessories are included at this price, since some listings bundle the charging dock and boundary markers while others treat them as separate purchases that push the real cost closer to the next price tier.

#### What do budget robot mowers compromise on?
Every budget model on this list makes a specific set of compromises rather than being uniformly worse than pricier machines. Some cap coverage tightly (100–200 m²) but include capable navigation for that smaller area; others stretch coverage further but with a simpler bump-sensor obstacle system rather than camera-based avoidance. Slope tolerance tends to sit lower across the budget tier — often 20–25% rather than the 35%+ seen on premium AWD models — which matters if any part of your lawn has a noticeable incline. App depth is the most consistently reduced feature: expect basic scheduling and manual zone drawing rather than the automated mapping and detailed cutting-pattern controls found on mid-range and premium machines. None of these compromises make a budget model unsuitable for its intended garden — they simply mean the machine is tuned for a specific, simpler job rather than being a scaled-down version of a premium all-rounder.

#### Is wire-free worth it at the budget end?
Budget wire-free models exist and have become genuinely competitive, using simpler camera-only or basic RTK systems rather than the hybrid setups found on premium machines. The trade-off is usually boundary precision in tricky conditions — shaded corners, close walls — where a budget wire-free model may need occasional manual correction that a premium hybrid system wouldn't. Budget wired models, by contrast, offer a fixed, reliable boundary at a lower hardware cost, at the expense of a day's installation labour and no flexibility if the garden layout changes later. For a simple, stable, open garden shape, either budget path works; for anything with awkward corners, the installation flexibility of wire-free usually outweighs the small accuracy trade-off. Installation labour is worth pricing in honestly if you're comparing a cheaper wired model against a pricier wire-free one, since a full day spent burying cable has a real cost even if it isn't on the receipt.

#### Where cutting corners costs you later
The genuine false economy in this price bracket isn't the mower itself but consumables and coverage mismatch. Replacement blades need changing every few months through a full Irish growing season, and budget models sometimes use proprietary blade shapes that cost more per replacement than the savings on the initial purchase price would suggest — check blade cost and availability before buying, not after. Buying a model rated right at your garden's exact size, rather than with headroom, is the second common mistake, since real-world coverage typically runs below the advertised figure once a garden has any obstacles or shape complexity, leaving an undersized budget mower struggling to keep up during peak May-June growth. Warranty terms are worth reading closely too, since some budget brands offer noticeably shorter cover than their mid-range models, which matters most for the battery — the single most expensive component to replace outside of warranty.

#### Getting the most from a budget machine
Two habits close most of the gap between a budget and mid-range result. First, use mulching mode by default rather than collecting clippings, since fine, frequent mulching keeps grass looking tidier than a budget mower's simpler cutting pattern would suggest on its own, and it's the default setting on nearly every model in this bracket anyway. Second, schedule shorter, more frequent sessions rather than trying to catch up with one long weekly run — budget mowers with smaller batteries and simpler navigation handle little-and-often far better than an infrequent heavy cut, which also suits Ireland's steady rather than spiky growth pattern through the season. Keeping the cutting deck and wheels free of built-up grass after wet sessions also matters more on a budget model, since simpler motors and bearings tend to be less tolerant of debris than the sealed units found on premium machines.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Is a budget robot mower worth it or should I save for a mid-range model?
A: For a straightforward garden under roughly 300 m² with a simple boundary and minimal slope, a budget model does the actual job competently and the extra spend on a mid-range mower mostly buys features — multi-zone mapping, AWD, sharper positioning — that a simple garden doesn't need. The case for saving up strengthens with garden complexity: a split layout, a noticeable slope, or a boundary with tight corners all expose budget-tier compromises more visibly. Match the decision to your specific garden's demands rather than a general rule, since a well-matched budget mower on a suitable garden often outperforms a mismatched mid-range one.

Q: What do you lose by buying under €700 versus a €1,200 mower?
A: The most consistent differences are navigation precision, slope tolerance and app sophistication. €1,200-range mowers more often include RTK-grade or hybrid camera-and-satellite positioning accurate to a few centimetres, AWD or higher slope ratings for uneven ground, multi-zone mapping for split gardens, and deeper app controls over cutting patterns and scheduling. Build quality and anti-theft features (GPS tracking, alarms) also tend to improve at this tier. What doesn't necessarily improve is basic cutting performance on a simple, flat, single-zone garden — the gap is mostly about handling complexity and edge cases rather than cut quality on straightforward ground.

Q: How long do batteries in budget robot mowers typically last?
A: Most budget models are rated for 300–500 full charge cycles before capacity noticeably declines, which translates to roughly two to four years of typical Irish seasonal use depending on how much of the growing season the mower runs actively. Battery degradation shows up as shorter run-times per charge and more frequent docking rather than sudden failure, so a mower that once ran 60 minutes per charge might drop to 40–45 minutes after a couple of seasons. Some budget models use a sealed, non-replaceable battery, while others allow a battery swap — worth checking before buying if you want to extend the mower's life past the typical degradation point.

Q: Are budget robot mowers reliable in heavy Irish rain?
A: Most budget models carry an IPX4 rating, the same baseline as premium machines, meaning they're built to handle drizzle and light-to-moderate rain without issue. Where budget models more often fall short is rain sensor quality — some use a simpler moisture sensor that pauses mowing later or resumes earlier than a premium unit's more calibrated version, occasionally cutting wet grass and leaving clumped clippings on the lawn surface. This is a minor cosmetic issue rather than a reliability concern, and checking owner reports specifically for rain-sensor behaviour is more useful than relying on the IP rating alone when comparing budget models.

Q: Can I upgrade a budget robot mower's app features later?
A: Generally no — the navigation hardware (GPS-RTK modules, cameras, sensor arrays) is fixed at purchase, so features like multi-zone mapping or advanced obstacle avoidance that depend on that hardware can't be added through a software update if the physical sensors aren't there. Some manufacturers do push firmware updates that improve scheduling logic, mulching patterns or minor app usability over a model's lifetime, so it's worth checking a brand's update history before buying, but treat any budget purchase as fixed in its core navigation capability rather than a stepping-stone that will gain premium features later.

# CATEGORY: Robot Vacuums
URL: https://pickireland.best/robot-vacuums/
5 guides, 32 product entries
==============================================================================

Robot vacuums crossed the believability line around 2023: modern lidar navigation actually maps your home, mops actually mop, and self-empty docks mean weeks without thinking about floors. Prices run €150 to €1,500, and the right answer depends on floors, pets and tolerance for occasional robot nonsense. We compare what each euro tier really buys in an Irish home.

## Lidar navigation is the dividing line
Sub-€200 robots mostly bounce randomly; lidar models map rooms, clean in neat rows, and let you say 'kitchen only' from the app. If the budget reaches €250, cross the lidar line — it's the single biggest experience upgrade.

## Suction numbers (Pa) are half-truths
Manufacturers quote Pascals (5,000–18,000 Pa), but brush design and airflow matter as much. Carpet homes need 5,000 Pa+; hard floors are easy for anything decent. Treat Pa as a tiebreaker, not a ranking.

## Self-empty docks change the relationship
Without one, you empty a tiny bin every run or two. With one, the robot empties itself for 4–8 weeks. For pet homes or busy households, the dock converts a gadget into an appliance. Budget €100–200 extra; worth it.

## Mopping: pads wipe, systems wash
Basic drag-a-damp-pad mopping freshens hard floors. Real mopping systems (rotating pads, self-washing docks) handle actual dirt. Irish homes with tiled kitchens and hallways get real value from the better systems — muddy paw season is long.

It brings that full-service Omni dock experience in under €500, slightly cheaper than the X10 Pro. Being a newer platform than the X10 line means less of a track record, and the docking station is just as bulky, needing dedicated floor space. A strong pick specifically for households that prioritise genuinely clean mopping over the X10's slightly more proven pedigree.

#### Why can't a robot vacuum clean an upstairs and downstairs on its own?
Robot vacuums don't climb stairs, full stop, and that single fact shapes the purchase more than any spec on the box. The typical Irish semi-detached or terraced house puts bedrooms on the first floor and kitchen and sitting room below, and a single robot only ever covers the level it's parked on. Owners either carry the unit between floors manually, buy a second cheaper unit for upstairs, or accept that one floor gets robot coverage and the other gets a stick vacuum on Saturdays. None of this is a flaw in any particular model; it's true of every robot vacuum sold, flagship or budget. Work out which floor genuinely needs the automation — usually the one with the most foot traffic or the pet — before comparing navigation systems or suction figures, because the floor-coverage question decides more about satisfaction than which lidar sensor is inside.

#### What do you actually gain moving up a robot vacuum tier?
Moving from budget to mid-range mainly buys you lidar or vision-based mapping instead of random-bounce navigation, which means rooms get covered systematically instead of by repeated overlapping passes — faster cleans, better battery use, and no-go zones you can actually draw on a floor plan. Moving from mid-range to premium buys automation depth, not raw cleaning power: self-emptying bins that stretch manual intervention from days to weeks, mop pads that wash and dry themselves instead of smearing dirty water around, and obstacle cameras that recognise cables and pet mess rather than just bumping into them. Suction figures published by manufacturers climb across all three tiers but matter far less in practice than brush design and floor-following behaviour. If your home is small, mostly hard floor, and lightly used, a mid-range lidar model usually does the job a flagship does, just with more manual bin-emptying — money spent on the top tier there buys convenience, not cleanliness.

#### Can one robot vacuum handle tile, wood and carpet in a single run?
Most Irish homes aren't one floor type — hallway and kitchen tile, sitting-room wood or laminate, bedroom and stairs-landing carpet — and a robot crossing all three in one run needs to adjust suction and brush behaviour automatically rather than being set once and left. Manufacturer spec sheets increasingly list carpet-boost or auto-detect suction as a named feature, worth checking for specifically rather than assumed. Deep-pile or older carpet also traps more than surface dust: in Ireland's damp climate, carpet holds moisture readily, and combined with pet hair or dust it becomes a slow mould risk if it's only vacuumed occasionally. A robot running a proper daily or alternate-day schedule keeps that buildup down far better than a weekly manual vacuum, which is one of the stronger arguments for automation on carpeted Irish homes specifically, rather than the hard-floor-heavy houses the marketing photos usually show.

#### Who honours a robot vacuum warranty in Ireland after Brexit?
Since Brexit, where a brand actually fulfils orders and spare parts from matters more than it used to. Some robot vacuum brands sell into Ireland from UK warehouses, which can mean customs friction and delay on replacement filters, brushes or dock bags; others run EU distribution that ships parts from within the bloc without the same paperwork. Before buying, it's worth checking whether the retailer or brand has an Irish or EU-based support line and returns address, not just a UK one — a two-year warranty is only as useful as the ease of actually using it. Irish electronics retailers stocking a brand directly, rather than a marketplace reseller, generally handle warranty claims faster than going back to an overseas manufacturer. This matters more the further up the price range you go, since premium units have more that can go wrong and pricier parts to replace.

#### What does a robot vacuum really cost over three years?
The sticker price is the smallest number in a robot vacuum's real cost. Manufacturer figures and part-store pricing put annual consumables — main brush, side brushes, filters, and for self-empty models a supply of dock bags — somewhere between roughly €80 and €150 a year depending on tier and how often the model needs replacements. Mop-equipped machines add pad wear and, on self-washing docks, cleaning solution on top of that. Electricity for a dock left on standby year-round is modest but not zero. Stretched across three years of ownership, a budget machine bought for €200 and a mid-range one bought for €400 can end up closer in total cost than the purchase price suggests, once the budget model's shorter part lifespan and higher failure-replacement rate are factored in. Treat the box price as a deposit on an ongoing running cost, not the full transaction.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Do I need a robot vacuum on every floor of a two-storey house?
A: No — most Irish two-storey homes get the most value from one unit on the ground floor, where daily foot traffic, kitchen crumbs and hallway grit accumulate fastest. Upstairs bedrooms and landings typically need vacuuming far less often, so a second robot is rarely worth the outlay unless there's a pet or heavy carpet upstairs too. Carrying a single unit up and down works in theory but rarely survives contact with a busy week — most owners who try it end up leaving the robot on one floor permanently within a month. If budget allows only one unit, put it where the mess actually happens, not where the carpet looks nicest.

Q: Does Wi-Fi actually matter, or is the app just a gimmick?
A: For basic scheduling, no — most robots will run a fixed daily time without ever opening the app again. Wi-Fi and the app matter for two things specifically: room-by-room mapping with no-go zones, and remote start when you're not home, both useful in Irish homes with irregular hours or a spare room used for storage that should be skipped. It also matters for firmware updates, which occasionally fix real navigation bugs. A patchy router signal in a solid-walled older Irish house can cause disconnects and missed schedules more often than the vacuum itself is at fault, so check Wi-Fi coverage in the room the dock sits in before assuming a fault with the machine.

Q: How noisy are robot vacuums, and does it matter for a small house?
A: Manufacturer figures typically list a range from around 55 dB on quiet or carpet-avoidance modes up to 65-70 dB on max suction — comparable to a conversation up to a running dishwasher. In a small terraced or semi-detached house, that's audible through most of the ground floor when it's running, which matters if you plan overnight or early-morning cleans near a bedroom close to the stairs. Running during the working day rather than at 6am avoids most complaints. Self-empty docks add a separate, louder burst of noise for 10-15 seconds during emptying, which some owners find more startling than the vacuum itself.

Q: What happens to a robot vacuum if the power goes out mid-clean?
A: It stops wherever it is and resumes the same cleaning cycle once power returns and it's had a chance to redock and recharge, assuming it has enough map memory to remember where it left off — true of essentially all lidar and vision-mapping models sold today. Older bump-navigation budget models without persistent maps may just restart the whole clean from the dock. Irish power cuts are infrequent but not unheard of in rural or coastal areas during winter storms; it's a minor consideration, not a deciding one, but worth knowing it won't damage the unit or lose your saved map.

Q: Should I wait for next year's model instead of buying now?
A: Robot vacuum navigation and mapping matured several years ago; the year-on-year changes now are mostly in obstacle-avoidance camera accuracy, dock automation and app polish rather than fundamental cleaning ability. A two- or three-year-old mid-range model with lidar mapping cleans a normal Irish home about as well as this year's equivalent. Waiting makes more sense if you specifically want a feature not yet available at your budget — cross-floor mapping memory, say — than as a general strategy, since prices on current-generation stock typically drop once a successor launches anyway.

#### What kind of navigation do you actually get under €300 now?
A few years ago, sub-€300 meant random-bounce navigation with no memory between cleans; that's no longer true across the board. Several budget-tier robots now ship with genuine lidar or basic vision mapping, giving room-by-room cleaning, resumable cleans after charging, and app-drawn no-go zones — features that were mid-range exclusives not long ago. What you still don't get at this price is the mapping precision or multi-floor memory of pricier models: budget lidar units typically hold one or two saved maps rather than several, and re-mapping after furniture moves takes longer. For a typical Irish terraced house or apartment with a fairly stable layout, that's rarely a practical problem. It becomes one if you rearrange furniture often or want separate saved maps for upstairs and downstairs — check the spec sheet's map-storage number specifically, not just whether it says smart navigation.

#### Mopping at this price is wiping, not washing
Nearly every budget robot vacuum under €300 that includes mopping does it with a static or vibrating pad dragged behind the unit, not a rotating, pressurised pad — the mechanism reserved for mid-range and premium models. That means it wipes rather than scrubs, fine for daily maintenance on tile or sealed wood to catch dust and light spills, but it won't shift dried-on marks or grease the way a proper mop would. Water flow is usually gravity-fed and can't be finely adjusted, so pad dampness varies as the tank empties across a clean. None of this is a defect at the price; it's simply what mopping means at this tier, and it's worth treating it as a bonus feature on top of vacuuming rather than a real substitute for occasional manual mopping in an Irish kitchen that sees muddy shoes and dog paws most of the year.

#### How much worse is obstacle avoidance under €300?
The clearest gap between budget and mid-range robots is obstacle handling, not suction. Budget units at this price mostly rely on basic infrared or bump sensors, which catch furniture legs and walls reliably but frequently miss low, soft, or dark obstacles — phone chargers, shoes left by the door, dark socks on a dark carpet, pet mess. Mid-range and premium models increasingly use small cameras with object recognition to identify and route around these specifically. For a genuinely tidy home with hard floors, this gap barely matters. For a home with kids, a dog, or a habit of dropping cables on the floor, it means more pre-clean tidying to avoid a tangled brush or a smeared mess, and it's the single biggest quality-of-life difference buyers moving up from this price bracket report first when they upgrade.

#### Budget self-empty docks: convenience with a catch
A handful of budget robots now include self-empty docks, extending manual bin-emptying from every clean to roughly every three to four weeks. It sounds like a mid-range feature at a budget price, and largely is one, but the dust bags themselves are a recurring cost worth budgeting for separately — typically sold in packs, running out to somewhere in the region of €15-20 for a few months' supply depending on how often the robot runs. The docks are also physically larger than a basic charging dock, which matters more than it sounds in a small Dublin terraced house or apartment where hallway or utility-room floor space is already tight. Measure the dock's footprint against your actual available floor space before assuming a self-empty budget model will fit where the old charging-only dock sat.

#### Is refurbished or outlet stock a safe way to stretch the budget?
Outlet, refurbished and previous-generation stock is one of the most reliable ways to get mid-range navigation and build quality for a genuinely budget price, provided the seller is clear about warranty terms. A previous year's mid-range model, discounted once its successor launches, frequently outperforms a current-year budget model on mapping precision and obstacle handling for similar or less money. The catch is warranty length and support — refurbished units often carry six or twelve months rather than the standard two years, and it's worth confirming whether that cover comes from an Irish or EU-based seller rather than a cross-border marketplace listing, given the parts-availability friction that's become more common since Brexit. Buying refurbished from an Irish retailer's own outlet section is generally safer than a third-party marketplace listing with vague provenance.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Is a €150 robot vacuum worth buying, or should I save for €300?
A: Below roughly €150, most models still use bump navigation without any mapping memory, meaning every clean starts from scratch with overlapping, inefficient passes and no no-go zones. That's a real functional gap, not just a missing nice-to-have — it means longer clean times, more missed spots, and no way to keep the robot out of a specific room. Between €150 and €300, lidar and basic mapping become common, which is where most of the practical usability jump happens. If the budget stretches to €250-300, it's generally worth it; below €150, you're often better off saving a bit longer or considering outlet stock on a discontinued mid-range model instead.

Q: Do budget robot vacuums handle multiple rooms well?
A: The mapping-equipped budget models handle multiple rooms reasonably well now, saving a room-by-room layout and letting you clean the kitchen only, say, rather than the whole floor. The gap shows up in map storage limits — most budget lidar units hold one or two maps rather than several, so a house with a complicated, irregular layout gets less benefit than a simple rectangular layout. Doorways with thick thresholds or steps between rooms, common in older Irish houses, can also confuse budget navigation more than premium sensors, occasionally leaving a room only partially covered.

Q: Are budget robot vacuum batteries good enough for a full house?
A: Manufacturer figures for sub-€300 models typically list 120-180 minutes of runtime, generally enough for a single-floor clean of an average Irish semi-detached or terraced house on one charge. Larger or more cluttered floor plans may need the auto-resume-after-charging feature to finish, which almost all current budget lidar models include. Battery degradation over two to three years of daily use is the more relevant long-term question — expect a noticeable runtime drop by year two on a budget cell, which is one area where the cost saving versus mid-range battery quality shows up most clearly.

Q: What's the most common complaint with budget robot vacuums in Ireland?
A: Beyond navigation, the recurring theme in owner reports is app reliability and Wi-Fi reconnection, particularly in older houses with solid or stone walls that weaken signal between rooms. The second most common issue is brush tangling on rugs with longer fringe or loose threads, since budget brush designs are less tangle-resistant than mid-range comb designs. Neither is usually a fault with the specific unit — they're consistent enough across budget-tier brands to be a category trait rather than a bad batch, and worth expecting rather than being surprised by after purchase.

Q: Can I add a self-empty dock later to a budget robot that doesn't have one?
A: No — self-empty docks are matched to a specific robot model's bin design and charging contacts, so there's no universal add-on that retrofits the feature onto a robot that shipped without it. If automated bin-emptying matters, it needs to be decided at purchase, either by choosing one of the budget models that now include a self-empty dock as standard, or accepting manual emptying and factoring that into which model you buy. Some brands sell the dock separately for the exact same model bought without one, but only within that same product line, never across brands or unrelated models.

#### Does brush design matter more than suction for pet hair?
For pet hair specifically, brush geometry matters more than the suction figure on the box. A rubber or silicone brush with raised comb ridges sheds wrapped hair back off itself as it spins, where a traditional bristle brush accumulates a tight knot around the axle that needs manual cutting free every week or two. Manufacturer spec sheets increasingly flag anti-hair-wrap brush designs by name — worth treating as a genuine buying criterion for pet homes rather than marketing language, since the difference in weekly maintenance time is significant. Long-haired breeds and double-coated dogs that shed heavily during seasonal changes put more strain on any brush design, budget or premium, so expect more frequent brush cleaning during spring and autumn coat-blow. It's worth checking a specific brush's design in product photos rather than trusting the tangle-free label alone, since the term gets applied loosely across the market.

#### How big a bin do you need in a pet household?
A pet household generates far more debris volume per clean than a pet-free one, which makes bin size — and for self-empty models, dock bag size — a more relevant spec than it is for other buyers. A robot with a small onboard bin in a heavy-shedding household can fill mid-clean on a large open-plan floor, forcing an early return to dock and an incomplete run. Self-empty docks solve this at the cost of more frequent dock-bag replacement — a large dog household can go through bags noticeably faster than the weeks-between-changes figure on the box, which is usually estimated for a lighter, average-shedding scenario. Checking a model's stated bin or bag capacity in litres, and cross-referencing it against your own pet's typical shedding volume, is worth doing before assuming the marketed emptying interval will hold in practice.

#### Why does cleaning frequency beat suction power for pet dander?
Ireland's damp climate keeps humidity in soft furnishings and carpet fibres higher for longer than in drier climates, and pet dander combined with that moisture is a specific irritant and mild mould-risk combination worth taking seriously in a pet home. Dander is fine enough to work down into carpet pile rather than sitting on the surface, which means infrequent vacuuming lets it accumulate rather than just sitting there waiting to be picked up. This is one case where a robot's real advantage over a manual vacuum isn't raw suction power but simple frequency — a daily or alternate-day automated clean keeps dander and hair from building up in carpet fibres in the first place, rather than trying to extract an established buildup every week or two with a manual machine. HEPA-grade filtration on the exhaust, standard on most current mid-range and premium units, matters more here than in a pet-free home, recirculating less fine dander back into the air.

#### How much faster do consumables wear in a multi-pet home?
Multi-pet households, or a single pet with the run of more than one floor, push every consumable and maintenance interval faster than the manufacturer's baseline figures, which are generally modelled on a single average-shedding pet. Two cats or a cat and a dog together in a two-storey Irish home effectively doubles hair volume on the floor the robot covers, shortening real-world intervals between brush cleaning, filter replacement and dock-bag changes correspondingly. Since a robot only cleans the floor it's docked on, a heavy-shedding pet with access to both floors of the house means one floor is getting daily hair removal and the other isn't, which shows up as a visible difference within a couple of weeks. Households in this position often find it worth prioritising the floor where the pet actually sleeps or spends the most time over strict upstairs-downstairs symmetry.

#### What happens if a robot vacuum meets cat litter or pet mess?
Cat litter tracked onto hard floors, and dog or cat mess encountered mid-clean, are the two scenarios pet owners worry about most, and they're handled very differently across the market. Litter is mostly a mechanical problem solved reasonably well by any decent brush and suction combination, though loose litter can occasionally jam a brush the way long hair does. Solid mess is a different order of problem entirely: only premium models with camera-based obstacle recognition specifically trained to identify and avoid pet waste offer real protection against it, and that's a named, checkable feature on spec sheets rather than a general smart-navigation claim. Budget and most mid-range models have no such recognition and will simply drive through anything low enough to clear their chassis, which is worth weighing heavily for a household with a young puppy or an elderly, less reliably house-trained pet.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Will a robot vacuum handle cat litter tracked outside the box?
A: Reasonably well on hard floors, where the combination of side brush sweeping litter into the suction path and a decent main brush picks most of it up without issue. Loose, fine litter can occasionally work into brush bearings over time the way hair does, so it's worth an occasional check even without visible tangling. On carpet or rugs near the litter box, expect less complete pickup, since fine granules can settle into pile fibres more stubbornly than hair does. Positioning the litter box on a hard-floor area the robot covers regularly, rather than on carpet, makes a noticeable practical difference to how well this works.

Q: How often does a pet owner need to clean the robot's brush by hand?
A: With a genuinely tangle-resistant comb-style brush, roughly every two to three weeks for a single average-shedding pet, based on owner reports across current mid-range and premium models. A traditional bristle brush, or a household with two pets or a heavy seasonal shedder, can need it weekly. It's a five-minute job with the tool most models include, but skipping it lets hair work down into the brush bearing where it's harder to remove and can eventually affect motor load. Treating brush cleaning as a fixed fortnightly task rather than waiting for visible tangling tends to keep maintenance time lowest overall.

Q: Does a robot vacuum replace regular carpet cleaning in a pet home?
A: No — it significantly reduces surface hair and loose dander buildup between deeper cleans, but it doesn't replace periodic proper carpet cleaning or shampooing, particularly in a damp Irish home where ground-in dander and moisture together are a genuine mould-risk combination over time. Robots also can't extract embedded dirt from deep-pile carpet the way a proper carpet cleaner can; their suction is tuned for daily maintenance and surface debris, not deep extraction. Most pet owners find a daily robot clean stretches the interval between manual deep-cleans considerably, but doesn't eliminate the need for one entirely, especially in carpeted bedrooms a pet sleeps in.

Q: Are pet hair robot vacuums noisier because of the stronger suction?
A: Not meaningfully — pet-hair-focused models mostly differ in brush design and filtration rather than raw suction power, so published noise figures sit in the same general range as standard models, roughly 55-70 dB depending on mode. Any brief noise increase tends to come from auto-boost modes that detect carpet or heavier debris and briefly increase suction, common to most current models regardless of pet-specific marketing. If noise near a pet that's nervous of the vacuum is a concern, checking for a genuinely low quiet or pet mode with reduced suction is more useful than comparing headline maximum suction figures between models.

Q: Do robot vacuums help with pet allergies in the house?
A: They can help meaningfully as part of a broader approach, mainly by keeping dander and hair from accumulating in carpet and soft furnishings through daily rather than weekly cleaning, and by trapping fine particles in a sealed HEPA-grade filter rather than recirculating them the way some upright vacuums do. They don't address dander already airborne or settled on furniture, curtains and bedding, which a robot vacuum never touches. For a genuinely allergic household member, a robot is a reasonable complement to a good air purifier and regular soft-furnishing washing, not a standalone solution on its own.

#### What's the difference between rotating, vibrating and static mop pads?
Three distinct mopping mechanisms are sold under the same mop-combo label, and they perform very differently. Static cloth pads, common at the lower end, are dragged behind the unit and rely entirely on dampness and friction — fine for dust, ineffective on anything dried-on. Vibrating pads add rapid back-and-forth motion to loosen light marks without scrubbing pressure. Rotating pads, reserved for mid-range and premium models, spin under downward pressure the way a manual scrubbing motion would, and are the only mechanism of the three that manufacturer spec sheets consistently describe as capable of lifting actual stains rather than just wiping surface dust. None of the three is a substitute for a hands-and-knees scrub of a genuinely dirty floor, but the gap between static and rotating in daily maintenance mopping is large enough to be worth checking specifically.

#### How do mop robots avoid soaking your carpet?
Every mop combo needs a strategy for carpet, since a wet pad dragged across carpet either soaks it or, worse, redistributes dirty water into the fibres. The two approaches on the market are lifting — the mop mechanism physically raises a few millimetres off the floor when the robot detects carpet — and avoidance, where the robot's map routes it around carpeted rooms entirely during a mopping run. Lifting is the more useful mechanism for a typical Irish home with carpet and hard floor on the same level, since it allows one continuous run to vacuum everywhere and mop only the hard-floor sections without needing two separate scheduled cleans. Avoidance-only models require carpeted rooms to be manually excluded from the mop schedule via the app, which works but adds a setup step lifting doesn't need. Checking which mechanism a specific model uses is more useful than trusting a generic carpet-safe label.

#### What does a self-washing dock actually save you?
Self-washing docks rinse the mop pad in hot or cold water and dry it with warm air between cleans, which solves the least pleasant part of mop-combo ownership: manually removing and rinsing a dirty pad, and the mildew smell that develops if a damp pad is left on the robot or in a drawer. It's a genuine quality-of-life upgrade, not just a premium-tier gimmick, particularly in an Irish home where a damp pad left sitting for even a day or two in typical indoor humidity can start to smell. What it doesn't solve is the underlying water tank — someone still needs to refill clean water and empty dirty water periodically, generally every one to two weeks depending on how often the mop runs, so self-washing reduces manual mop-handling but doesn't eliminate all human involvement in the mopping cycle.

#### What does mopping add to a robot vacuum's running cost?
Mopping adds a running cost vacuuming alone doesn't have: cleaning solution or detergent, sold as an add-on by most brands offering self-washing docks, plus more frequent mop pad replacement than the vacuum-only brush and filter schedule. Manufacturer-recommended detergent isn't strictly required — plain water works for daily maintenance mopping — but brands market their own solution as improving grease-cutting on kitchen floors specifically, and using it adds a modest ongoing cost on top of the vacuum-only consumables already budgeted for elsewhere. Replacement mop pads themselves, sold in packs, are a relatively small addition to overall running costs but do wear out faster with heavier daily use, particularly on rotating-pad models where the pad experiences physical friction rather than just dampness. Factoring in an extra ongoing amount specifically for mopping consumables, on top of standard vacuum maintenance, gives a more honest running-cost picture than looking at vacuum-only figures alone.

#### Where mopping genuinely earns its keep in an Irish home
Mopping earns its keep fastest in Irish kitchens and hallways — tiled or sealed-wood entryways that take the brunt of eight-plus months of wet shoes a year, and kitchen floors exposed to daily cooking splashes and pet water-bowl spills. A hallway that catches rain-wet shoe prints daily benefits from a genuine daily light mop far more than a spare room that sees occasional foot traffic, which is worth factoring into which rooms actually get scheduled for mopping rather than mopping the whole floor plan by default. It earns its keep slowest on rooms with minimal traffic or on floor types unsuited to it — natural unsealed wood or certain stone floors can be damaged by regular damp mopping, so checking floor-type compatibility before scheduling mop runs there matters more than the mopping mechanism itself.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Will a robot mop damage real wood floors?
A: It depends on the finish, not the wood itself — sealed or engineered wood with a proper lacquer or oil finish generally tolerates light, well-wrung robot mopping fine, since the moisture level used is deliberately low. Unsealed, oiled-only, or older worn wood floors are more vulnerable to water damage over repeated exposure, and manufacturer guidance for most brands explicitly recommends excluding these floor types from scheduled mopping via the app's room settings. If in doubt about a specific floor's finish, checking with the flooring manufacturer or installer is safer than assuming the robot's water level is automatically low enough to be harmless everywhere.

Q: Does the mop pad need washing separately even with a self-washing dock?
A: Most models, most of the time, no — a working self-washing dock rinses the pad thoroughly enough for continuous reuse across many cleans without manual intervention. Owner reports do mention that grease or heavier kitchen residue can build up gradually even with automated rinsing, meaning an occasional manual hand-wash every few weeks keeps the pad performing at its best rather than slowly declining. This is a maintenance-quality issue rather than a fault — the automated rinse cycle is genuinely doing most of the work, but it's not infinitely self-sufficient on a heavily used kitchen floor.

Q: Can a mop combo leave streaks on tile floors?
A: Occasionally, particularly with harder water, which is common in parts of Ireland with limestone-heavy groundwater, since mineral deposits in tap water can leave a faint film after repeated mopping with plain water. Using a small amount of manufacturer-approved detergent generally reduces this, as does periodically wiping the floor manually to catch any buildup the robot's pad redistributes rather than fully lifts. It's a cosmetic issue rather than a functional one, and considerably less noticeable on matte or textured tile than on high-gloss polished tile, where any residue shows more readily under light.

Q: Is a vacuum-only robot plus a separate manual mop cheaper overall than a combo?
A: Often yes on upfront cost, since a decent vacuum-only lidar model plus an inexpensive manual spray mop can cost less than a mid-range combo unit, though it trades away the daily automated mopping the combo provides. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how often the floors actually need mopping — a household with mostly carpet and light hard-floor traffic gains little from an automated mop and is better served putting the budget difference toward a better vacuum-only unit instead. A household with heavy kitchen and hallway traffic gets more genuine daily value from the combo's automation than the price difference would suggest.

Q: How much water does a robot mop use per clean?
A: Manufacturer figures vary by tank size and mopping mode, but a typical mid-size tank on a moderate mopping setting covers roughly 80-150 square metres before needing a refill, broadly enough for one full ground-floor run in an average Irish semi-detached or terraced house. Larger open-plan layouts or a setting using more water per pass may need a mid-clean refill, which most current models pause for and resume automatically once topped up via the dock's water tank rather than requiring the whole clean to be restarted from scratch.

#### What does ‘six to eight weeks unattended’ actually require from a robot vacuum?
The weeks-of-unattended-operation figure premium brands advertise combines three systems working together: a large-capacity base bin, a water and detergent reservoir sized for repeated mop washes, and a dust bag or bin large enough to hold weeks of debris. A heavy-shedding pet or a large open-plan floor plan fills the bin faster than the manufacturer's baseline testing scenario, which assumes a moderate, average household. Reading the spec sheet's stated bin capacity in litres, and comparing it honestly against your own floor size and pet situation, gives a more realistic estimate of your actual emptying interval than trusting the headline number on the box, which is best case rather than typical case.

#### How good is obstacle AI on premium robot vacuums, really?
Camera-based obstacle recognition on premium models genuinely does what mid-range infrared sensors can't — identifying and routing around cables, shoes, pet mess and low furniture legs by shape rather than just detecting that an object is present. Manufacturer figures on recognition accuracy have climbed significantly over recent generations and owner reports consistently mention markedly fewer stuck-robot incidents than budget or mid-range models produce. The limits worth knowing: recognition confidence typically drops in low light, since most systems rely partly on the camera rather than purely on infrared or lidar depth-sensing, and very low, flat objects — a phone charger cable lying flat, a thin sock — remain harder to reliably distinguish from floor texture than upright obstacles. It's a substantial real improvement over lower tiers, not a guarantee of zero incidents, and worth treating that way when deciding how much pre-clean tidying is still needed.

#### Does multi-floor mapping solve the stairs problem?
Premium models generally store multiple floor maps and switch between them automatically when manually carried to a different level, a genuine practical advantage for a two- or three-storey Irish house over budget models limited to one saved map. What this doesn't solve is the fundamental stairs problem every robot vacuum shares: none climb them, so multi-floor map memory helps once you've carried the unit upstairs, but it doesn't carry the unit there itself. For a two-storey semi-detached house, this is a manageable inconvenience — carry it up occasionally, or accept ground-floor-only coverage most of the time. For a three-storey townhouse, common in parts of Dublin, it means either genuinely carrying a several-kilogram unit up two flights regularly, or buying a second unit for the top floor, both worth budgeting for honestly before assuming premium multi-floor mapping alone solves a three-storey layout.

#### What do premium robot vacuum consumables cost a year?
Premium tier consumables run higher than mid-range across every category — larger and more complex main brushes, HEPA filters rated for finer particles, rotating mop pads that wear faster under pressure than static ones, dock dust bags sized for the larger bin, and detergent for self-washing docks. Combined, manufacturer part pricing and independent cost breakdowns put a realistic annual figure noticeably above the roughly €80-150 range typical of simpler models, particularly in the first year when a full set of consumables may need replacing close together. Against that, the automation genuinely reduces time spent on maintenance tasks, which is the actual trade being made — premium tier costs more in parts to save more in manual labour, not to clean meaningfully better than a well-specified mid-range unit on the same floor.

#### Who should not buy a premium robot vacuum?
This tier is a poor fit for a heavily stepped three-storey house where a single unit can only cover the floor it's parked on regardless of how advanced its dock is — the premium features solve bin-emptying and mop-washing, not stairs, and a household in that situation is often better served by two simpler mid-range units, one per main floor, than one premium unit carried between three levels. It's also poor value for a small, tidy, mostly-hard-floor apartment or terraced house with minimal clutter and no pets, where a mid-range lidar model with basic obstacle avoidance already handles the actual cleaning load fine and the premium dock's weeks-of-autonomy advantage goes largely unused. The tier earns its price in larger, busier, pet-owning households with complex floor plans where the automation genuinely offsets real weekly maintenance time — not as a default upgrade for a simple home.

#### Frequently asked questions
Q: Is a premium robot vacuum worth it for a small apartment?
A: Generally not — the tier's main advantages are automation depth for larger, more complex, or heavily-used homes, and a small apartment with a simple floor plan and light daily mess doesn't generate enough cleaning volume to make weeks-long dock autonomy meaningful. A mid-range lidar model handles a compact one- or two-bedroom apartment's actual cleaning load about as well, at meaningfully lower upfront and consumable cost. The exception is a small apartment with genuinely no floor space for frequent manual bin-emptying or storage for cleaning supplies, where the dock's self-sufficiency has practical value beyond just cleaning performance.

Q: How much floor space does a premium self-empty dock actually need?
A: More than people expect — premium docks combining a large dust bin, water tank and sometimes a drying unit are noticeably bulkier than a basic charging dock, often requiring a dedicated corner with clearance on multiple sides for the robot to dock reliably. In a small Dublin terraced house or apartment, this can be a genuine constraint worth measuring against actual available space — hallway or utility room corners — before purchase, rather than assuming it will fit wherever the previous, simpler dock sat. Some brands publish dock dimensions on the spec sheet specifically for this reason, worth checking before ruling a space in or out.

Q: Do premium robot vacuums need an active Wi-Fi and app subscription?
A: Wi-Fi connectivity, yes, essentially always, since multi-floor mapping, obstacle-recognition updates and remote scheduling all depend on it. A paid ongoing subscription is not standard across the category the way it is for some smart-home cameras — most current premium brands include full app functionality with the purchase price, though a few have introduced optional paid tiers for extras like extended cloud map storage or AI feature updates. Checking a specific brand's current policy before buying is worthwhile, since this has shifted model to model and isn't yet a settled industry norm either way.

Q: Does obstacle-avoidance AI work as well in a dim room or at night?
A: Somewhat less reliably, based on manufacturer specifications and owner reports — most premium obstacle-recognition systems rely at least partly on an onboard camera, which performs better with adequate ambient light than in a dark room or overnight run. Many premium models include a small headlight to compensate, and lidar or infrared depth-sensing continues working regardless of light level for basic navigation, but object-identification accuracy specifically can drop after dark. Scheduling cleans during daylight or well-lit hours, rather than very early morning or late at night, generally gets closer to the manufacturer's best-case obstacle-avoidance performance.

Q: Do premium robot vacuums hold their resale value?
A: Reasonably, within the first two to three years — premium models from established brands tend to hold a higher proportion of original price on the Irish secondhand market than budget models, since buyers specifically seeking mapping and automation features are willing to pay more for used premium stock than for a new budget unit. Value drops off faster once a brand releases a clear successor generation with materially better obstacle AI or dock capacity, which happens roughly every one to two years at this tier. Keeping original accessories and the box generally helps resale more for this category than for simpler vacuum-only models, since buyers often want to confirm full dock functionality is intact.
